Mr. JEAN-FRANCOIS POULIOT (Temis-couata) (Translation): Mr. Speaker, at the opening of this sitting, I wish to correct the text of Question No. 38. The subject mentioned therein deals with the UB.S.R., in French the "U.R.SS., Union des Republiques Sovietiques Socialistes," such as Russia is now called.
In the seventh number of the Votes and Proceedings of the House of Commons, (French version), U.R.R.S. appears four times instead of U.R.S.S. It is almost as if you said "Cadana" instead of "Canada." There are four errors, two Rs, instead of two Ss, each time.
In the French version of the Routine Proceedings and Orders of the Day, under No. S, that same question No. 38 refers, the first time, to the U.R.S.S.-which is correct-and three other times to the U.R.R.S.: three additional errors, making a total of seven errors in the French version of the Votes and Proceedings and the Routine Proceedings and Orders of the Day for the same question. I have here the original text which I compared with these two officials documents that contain seven errors.
Speaking to a question of privilege, I have before me the votes, and proceedings of the House of Commons, No. 7 of January 25. I refer to question No. 38 on the orders of the day. The Union of Soviet Socialist Republics is referred to as "U.R.S.S.", but the correct designation in English is "U.S.S.R." and this is the designation we find in the Monthly Summary of the League of Nations. There are six mistakes in that question as it appears in issue No. 7 of the votes and proceedings. "U.R.S.S." is mentioned four times. This is the correct designation in French but it is the wrong one in English. Further, Mr. Maxim Litvinoff is referred to as "peoples Commissary in Foreign Affairs of the U.R. S.S." The word "peoples" should have a capital P and an apostrophe, "People's" and he is not Commissary in Foreign Affairs but Commissary for Foreign Affairs of the U.S.
S.R. I take this designation from the Monthly Summary of the League of Nations, issue of September, 1934.
I have just mentioned in French that there were nine mistakes in that question in French; there are six more in the votes and proceedings, making a total of fifteen mistakes. But

Questions
there are more mistakes than that because in the Routine Proceedings and Orders of the Day the same question contains the same mistakes. This is most ridiculous because the French designation of what was formerly Russia is wrong in the French text and the French designation of it has been used in the English text so that it is wrong again. May I draw attention to the fact that in that question there are twenty-one mistakes. I shall not stress this any more because the translator who was responsible has been discharged. But I make one suggestion and it is this: that every piece of translation should be initialed in order that every member might know who is responsible for the mutilation of his text whenever such occurs.
And now, sir, may I have the great pleasure of welcoming to this house our Quebec leader, Hon. Mr. Lapointe.

Has the Canada Shipping Act of 1934, chapter 44, been put into force?

I think an oral answer to this question will better serve the purpose.
As the house knows, the Canada Shipping Act, 1934, covers international, inter-empire and domestic matters. As to the domestic matters, such as part V, sick mariners and marine hospitals; part VI, pilotage; part IX, lighthouses, buoys and beacons on Sable island; part X, public harbours and harbour masters; part XI, port wardens, and so forth; it can be proclaimed at any time, and the question of doing so is now under consideration.
Why all the hurry last year?

As to international and inter-empire matters, as this was the first enactment dealing with merchant shipping to be undertaken by any dominion since the passing of the statute of Westminster, it will be utilized as a guide by other dominions when legislating in regard to merchant shipping, so that the desired measure of uniformity recommended by the conference on the operation of dominion legislation and Merchant Shipping Legislation of 1929, and the terms of the British commonwealth merchant shipping agreement of 1931 may be secured. The act I understand is now being examined from this point of view. No other dominions have yet enacted similar legislation. I may also point out that the conclusions of the international conference regarding safety of life at sea and load lines, which formed a large part of the act of 1934, have already been given effect to by this parliament, in August 1931, by chapter 49 of that year, and are in operation now.
I think this statement will serve as an answer to the query of the hon. member for New Westminster on January 21.
Would the minister at the same time answer as to that part of the act dealing with navigation on the great lakes, and the coastal laws?
As I stated, the subject is now under consideration, as to all parts of the act that concern domestic matters.
In other words, in the doldrums. It has been on the statute books two years.

speakeroldname: Mr. J. S. WOODSWORTH (Winnipeg North Centre) moved:
subtopic: PROPOSAL FOR APPOINTMENT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE TO CONSIDER AMENDMENTS
speechtext:
That, in the opinion of this house, a special committee should be set up to study and report on the best method by which the British North America Act may be amended so that while safeguarding the existing rights of racial and religious minorities and legitimate provincial claims to autonomy, the dominion government may be given adequate power to deal effectively with urgent economic problems which are essentially national in scope.
He said: Mr. Speaker, on March 20, 1924, I introduced a motion urging amendments to the British North America Act. Again on May 11, 1931, I introduced a somewhat similar motion. Perhaps at this time it is hardly necessary for me to cover the ground covered on those previous occasions. Possibly the discussion which took place in 1931 might be summed up by two quotations, one from the speech by the Minister of Justice (Mr. Guthrie) and the other from the speech of the hon. member for Quebec East (Mr. Lapointe)
At page 1477 of Hansard the Minister of Justice is reported as follows:
I think it would be well for this parliament if not at this session, at some subsequent session, to appoint a committee specially charged with the consideration of this question. We must prepare our case here before we call a conference, and it is a case that will require a great deal of preparation. . . . We must know in the first instance what we are prepared to agree on ourselves. Having reached that point I shall heartily favour the summoning of a conference of the provinces with the dominion authorities to see what plan can be worked out so that in the future this parliament may be able to make the necessary amendments to our constitution.
Hon. members will note that on that occasion the Minister of Justice definitely suggested the appointment of a special committee to deal with the question. I am now

B.N.A. Act-Mr. Woodsworth
following his lead and urging upon the house the appointment of such a committee. On the same day the hon. member for Quebec East made the following statement appearing at page 1479 of Hansard:
Again I say that to insist on having the consent of all the provinces to every change would be asking almost an impossibility; to ask that either British Columbia in the west or Prince Edward Island in the east should be able to block a change with which it is essential for the federal power to go ahead within the limits of its jurisdiction on certain matters, I do not think would be right; but on essential matters, such matters, for instance, as the protection of minorities, of language, of schools, as they are inserted in the British North America Act. I believe it should not be possible to make a change without the consent of all.
Notwithstanding the practical acceptance by the government of my resolution nothing definite has been done in the past four years. It is true that about the end of August of last year the Prime Minister suggested calling a conference to deal especially with this question, but that conference was finally postponed indefinitely. Despite that fact there is now greater need than ever for some amendments to the British North America Act. There is no doubt that jurisdiction disputes involve a great deal of litigation. I shall not go into that matter in detail to-day but would refer the house to my speech delivered in 1931 in which I somewhat exhaustively outlined the jurisdiction disputes which were occurring.
Further, there is a certain amount of overlapping which inevitably involves inefficiency and waste. Now that economy is being stressed it would seem that one way in which we could well economize would be in seeing that there are no unnecessary overlapping of departments. Then, the financial arrangements between the dominion and the provinces are very unsatisfactory. The provinces are called upon to undertake many new services. At the time of the drawing up of the British North America Act it was not contemplated governments would be expected to deal with many matters now being forced upon them. At the present time many social services are given which were not even remotely dreamed of at the time of confederation, and this condition places a burden upon the provinces which they are not able to continue to bear.
Further, the taxing power of the provinces is strictly limited. Hon. members know that they cannot resort to indirect taxation, and we know also that the dominion government has entered the field of income tax. For these reasons it is extremely difficult for the provinces to meet the requirements of the

new services being undertaken. I think, too, it is manifest that the wealth has been concentrated in the central provinces. I have sometimes heard representatives from Montreal or Toronto talk as if they were carrying the whole burden of the dominion. It may very well be that residents of the two central provinces, pay a large proportion of the income tax, but I would point out that the central provinces are able to draw to no very small extent upon the west. They have a mortgage, as it were, upon the west, and also to a large extent on the east. Take the banks, for example. The central offices of all the banks in Canada are located in Montreal or Toronto, and thus they can assist in paying taxes here whereas their branches out in either western Canada or eastern Canada cannot be levied upon in the same way. That same thing is true to a very large extent of a great many of our big industrial and commercial concerns. Without going into this matter at any length I would refer to some very excellent articles which appeared in the Canadian Forum of November and December last by N. MacL. Rogers.
Again I would point out that there is need for uniformity in connection with social legislation. With the program which is being introduced at the present time by the government I fancy it will be found necessary, if not to amend tJ'd British North America Act, at least to adopt other interpretations than hitherto have been invoked. But whether or not the program of the government can be put through without amending the British North America Act, there are a great many other matters which are very pressing at the present time and which would seem to be halted because of the existence of this antiquated constitution of ours. Anyone who has been present in the house during these past years must know that hardly a measure is ever brought forward looking to greater efficiency in carrying on the affairs of the dominion but what some member on this or the other side of the house will arise and flourish the British North America Act in our faces.
We need to have uniformity with regard to a great many of these social services, and here I would venture to call to my assistance no other than Premier Taschereau himself who, speaking in Montreal on December 17 last, in referring to a complaint that Quebec fruit was competing with British Columbia fruit in*the British Columbia market, said:
As a Canadian I think that the dominion from Cape Breton to British Columbia is my country.

B.N.A. Act-Mr. Woodsworth
I am glad to hear Mr. Taschereau uttering sentiments of that kind. I hope he will take the same position in regard to various types of social legislation. If we are to have anything like equality of opportunity in trade matters, surely we should have some equality in regard to the conditions under which goods are being produced. Without going into the details of the evidence before the price spreads committee I think it is manifest that if any one province is backward in its conditions of labour, that inevitably makes it very difficult for other provinces to institute reforms. It does seem to me that in recent years we have been permitting the provinces to claim rights that should never have been accorded them. When the British North America Act was drawn up the residual power, as we all know, was placed in the hands of the dominion government. I believe even under the clause dealing with the residual power the dominion government in the past could have done very much more than the former Liberal government or the Conservative government have done. In cases of emergency, the Relief Act, for instance, was brought into force, and although not as much was done for the unemployed as might have been done, there was certain relief given to the bankers and some big industrial concerns.
There is no reason whatever why the dominion government under the residual clause should not act in giving effect to treaties and conventions. Throughout the past years, without going into fine legal questions, I have again and again taken the ground that if the dominion government has the authority to sign a peace treaty, then it surely has the power to see that the provisions of that treaty are carried out, that the treaty is implemented by legislation. I am glad to note that some recent decisions of the privy council seem to give support to this view. Professor F. R. Scott, in speaking of the radio broadcasting case, says this:
The privy council held that power to enforce these treaties fell within the dominion residuary clause. This may prove to be a judgment of great importance. It seems to leave the way open for dominion control of any aspect of the internal life of Canada, so long as the matter is covered by an international agreement to which Canada is a party -
If the dominion government decides to adhere to a trade convention agreed upon by the labour office, there is a strong ground, since the radio case, for supposing that her adherence would give parliament the same power to pass implementing legislation as the radio judgment says it possesses in regard to ordinary conventions.
That statement will be found at page eight of a pamphlet entitled Social Reconstruction, by Professor Scott.
I think, Mr. Speaker, that all sections of the house will agree that the British North America Act needs amending, and that in itself is a considerable advance on the contention that prevailed a few years ago. Further I think it is fairly generally conceded that the consent of the provinces is not necessary, at least from the legal standpoint. There was a time when we were told that we could not amend the British North America Act without the consent of all the provinces, that in fact confederation was something in the nature of a treaty and that it could not be changed without the consent of all parties. I think that theory has been absolutely discarded, and we need not continue to debate it. The Prime Minister, during the debate in this house on the Relief Act, on April 13, 1934, in answer to Mr. Han-bury's question whether any amendment could be made where there was not unanimity, said at page 2163:
Two answers could be given to that question; one is the political answer and the other is the legal answer. The legal answer is that if this parliament-and that means both houses

adopts a resolution embodying a petition to the sovereign for the enactment of legislation by the parliament at Westminster amending the British North America Act, under the statute of Westminster such legislation would be enacted accordingly.
That is clear, very clear-cut indeed. Let me read the latter part of it again:
The legal answer is that if this parliament -and that means both houses-adopts a resolution embodying a petition to the sovereign for the enactment of legislation by the parliament at Westminster amending the British North Amercia Act, under the statute of Westminster such legislation would be enacted accordingly.

speechtext: Who said that?

subtopic: PROPOSAL FOR APPOINTMENT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE TO CONSIDER AMENDMENTS
speechtext:
That was said by the Prime Minister, speaking in this house on April 13, 1934. The Prime Minister goes on:
I referred to the political argument the other day. The constitution of Canada is a compromise, and the extent to which variations of that constitution should be effected, if they impinge upon the rights of the provinces that were the original partners to the confederation pact, is a matter that would require careful consideration.
The legal point is clear: It is a matter of expediency, the desire that there should be no injustice done to any one of the parties to confederation. I take it that the leader of the opposition comes very near to that position. Only the other day, on January 21,
B.N.A. Act-Air. Woodsworth

1935, at page 67 he admitted that the British North America Act required to be amended in some particulars. He suggested that the first amendment that should be secured was the right of this country to amend its own constitution. He called attention to the fact that Canada was the only country in the British dominions that had not that right, and he said:
I believe that the way to effect that change is by conference and by securing consent and agreement if at all possible. At all events that should be the first step.
He is not as definite as I should like him to be and as usual he surrounds his speech with a great many safeguarding clauses. But if I read that declaration correctly, it means that he concedes the legal right of parliament to go ahead, though for the sake of expediency a first step would be to secure if possible, as he says, the consent of the provinces.
In the past the procedure has not been altogether clear. The mode of procedure was one of the matters to have been discussed at the conference that was summoned by the Prime Minister. I would point out that the constitution was once amended by the British parliament on the strength of a simple request by the Canadian government without the proposal even coming before parliament. A great many people have the idea that the British North America Act is like the law of the Medes and Persians, that it can never be changed. But we forget the very large number of amendments that have already been made in the act. Once a request which was made by the dominion parliament carried the formal endorsation of eight out of the nine provinces and was opposed by one province. On the other occasions the British parliament acted on the joint request of the Canadian House of Commons and the Senate. The precedents therefore suggest that the British parliament will enact any legislation to amend the British North America Act on the recommendation of the Canadian parliament. That I think is the position we have arrived at. We need not fear opposition from the parliament at Westminster, and if we proceed in this parliament to petition the British government I have not the slightest doubt that that government will accede to the request.

Supposing we should pass a resolution in this huuse and the Senate refused to acquiesce? That I admit would be a rather serious situation, but I cannot conceive that for any length of time the upper chamber would be able to thwart the will of the Canadian people as represented by the elected chamber. On this point I was very happy the other day to come across a statement by Mr. Bennett, now Prime Minister. In 1915 in the House of Commons, on the occasion of the Senate declining to agree to an address for an immediate change in representation in that chamber, the present Prime Minister denounced the Senate, as will be seen by reference to page 2338 of Hansard. He referred to the upper house as an "irresponsible body which thwarted the will of democracy as expressed by this House of Commons." I submit that if the Senate should continue to thwart the will of the house, then undoubtedly the Senate would have to be overridden.
My motion is in keeping with the principle laid down in the Quebec resolution of the fathers of confederation:
That there be a general government charged with matters of common interest to the whole country and local governments for each of the provinces charged with control of local matters in their respective sections.
Now may I call attention to the terms of the resolution. The resolution is so clearly drawn and has such adequate safeguards, and moreover it is so eminently reasonable that I cannot see any reason why any section of the house should not accept it. I ask for a committee because it seems to me that it might very well be that it would help the government and perhaps promote the speedy passage of a measure of this kind if the public could be educated on the many complex questions that may arise. Here in the house we have a chance of discussing the matter, but we cannot very well call in experts who might give us some valuable advice. I have no fear of public discussion of matters of this kind. The more it is discussed the more clear it will be that some kind of amendment must come. I think I have stated the safeguards and I fancy that no one will quarrel with them:
that while safeguarding the existing rights of racial and religious minorities and legitimate provincial claims to autonomy ...
None of us is asking that any of the minorities shall suffer in any emendation of the British North America Act. Personally I would very gladly have a sort of bill of rights

B.N.A. Act-Mr. Guthrie
inserted in the very forefront of any constitution that might be drawn up, granting full religious and racial rights to minorities. I do not see where any of our friends from any one of the provinces can object to an emendation which would safeguard minorities in this way. But I would point out that we do need some means of dealing with very many of the practical problems that come before us. I would be among the very first in giving credit to the fathers of confederation for the great work they did in their day. The fact that we want to amend the instrument they drew up is no reflection on the work they did. I submit however that Canada has travelled a long distance in the past sixty-five years. Conditions are very different in this country from what they were sixty-five years ago. A whole series of social problems has arisen in that time. Canada has been linked together by its great railways, and it is intimately linked together by the radio. Companies have branches in every province and commerce flows back and forth. It is thus manifest that along many lines legislation to be effective must be dominion-wide in character. It is for this reason, in order to bring legislation up to the economic development of the time, that I would ask for an emendation of the British North America Act. If the fathers of confederation had ability enough to draw up an instrument which served their day and generation, it seems to me that we their grandchildren ought to have brains and common sense enough to amend it in such a way that it may serve the needs of the people to-day.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: PROPOSAL FOR APPOINTMENT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE TO CONSIDER AMENDMENTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the motion which has
been placed in your hands by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Woods-worth) raises a subject which is not entirely new to this house. I grant at the outset that it is a very important subject and one quite worthy of discussion by this house or by a
special committee, the appointment of which is the object sought in this motion.
The question of amendment of the Canadian constitution involves many considerations and some serious difficulties. I am aware that even in the days when the constitution was drafted, when the original conferences took place, there was a cleavage of opinion. There was a school of thought which advocated in this country a legislative union whereby all provinces should be brought together in one parliament. There was another school of thought which advocated a federal system such as was subsequently established. It can be very ably argued and was argued very forcefully to-day that perhaps a legislative union might have enabled this parliament to solve many of the difficulties with which we are beset from time to time, because under such a system this parliament would have had full power to legislate as it saw fit for all parts of Canada. But the other view, that of a federal system, was finally adopted and an agreement or treaty was executed by the representatives of the various parts of Canada who were assembled at conferences in 1864, 1865 and 1866 providing that a federal system should be adopted in Canada upon certain specific terms. That agreement or treaty was carried into the act of parliament which we know as the British North America Act passed by the parliament at Westminster.
The question arises: How can we amend or change our constitution if we desire so to do? It is a singular fact that in the British North America Act there is no power which will permit the parliament of Canada to amend it and it is most notable that in all subsequent dominion constitutions which have been granted by the parliament of Great Britain to dominions situated in conditions similar to those in which we live, a specific power of amendment has been incorporated in the various ants. The Canadian constitution was the first constitutional act which was adopted by the parliament at Westminster in regard to colonial government, and to a large extent it became the model of all other constitutions which were subsequently granted by the Imperial parliament. It is therefore the more notable that in all subsequent constitutions, namely in those of Australia, New Zealand, South Africa and the Irish Free State there has been included in the various constitutional acts an express power enabling these dominions to amend their own constitutions but with some limitations in regard to some of those enactments. I think it may be assumed from the fact that such a power is not included in the British North America Act that the omission did not arise through oversight

B.N.A. Act-Mr. Guthrie
but by design. It was a matter that was definitely decided; the power to amend was omitted after consideration and as a matter of agreement. The chief reason for the omission of power of amendment was to be found no doubt in a realization of the fact that Canada was a country populated very largely by two distinct races and considerably divided upon religious questions. It was for the express purpose of protecting the rights of minorities that power to amend our constitution was not granted to the parliament of Canada when the British North America Act was passed.
The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre in his interesting discussion of the subject has intimated that in his opinion the Canadian parliament should have power to amend the constitution subject to certain limitations as expressed in his resolution, and I am to a large extent in accord with the opinion which he has offered in that respect. He has pointed out that in one and perhaps in more than one instance the British parliament has passed amendments to the British North America Act upon the joint address of the House of Commons and the Senate and also in one instance simply upon the request of the government of Canada. I think it has always been admitted that in regard to mere matters of form and matters of procedure the parliament of Great Britain would in all cases pass an amendment to the British North America Act if requested so to do, upon the joint address of the Senate and the House of Commons. However, that is only a minor branch of the subject. Matters of form and matters of procedure are unimportant. In 1895 I think some doubt arose as to the power of this parliament to appoint a deputy speaker of the House of Commons. That matter was referred to the parliament of Great Britain and immediately an amendment was passed by the British parliament confirming the action taken by the parliament of Canada. That might be called merely a question of procedure, and I have no doubt that the parliament at Westminster would at all times respond in such matters to the request of the Senate and the House of Commons of Canada.
But where an amendment is sought which goes to the basis of the original treaty or agreement which was made at the time of confederation, or where the fundamental principles upon which we were originally brought together, are involved, I doubt very much whether the parliament at Westminster would entertain a request of that nature based solely upon an address from the Senate and House of Commons. I know it has been argued by 
some very able men that the parliament at Westminster would grant any request for amendment made by the Senate and House of Commons irrespective of the views of the provinces. They argue that all the provinces of Canada are represented in this parliament; that all provinces may speak and vote here and that if the House of Commons and the Senate decide that an address shall be presented, such action is binding upon all the provinces through their representatives in this parliament. Personally I do not take that view of the matter. The provinces of Canada constituted by the British North America Act, are in the nature of sovereign states so far as the affairs which have been committed to them by section 92 of the British North America Act are concerned. In regard to the subjects allotted to them they are supreme and their powers are just as plenary and complete as those of this parliament in dealing with matters which have been placed under federal control.
Section 92 of the act sets forth in the first lines that the following named subjects shall be exclusively within the control of the provincial legislatures. If we sought by amendment to alter the basis of confederation, by taking from section 92 any of the subjects given exclusively to the provinces, or by interfering with any subjects exclusively placed under the jurisdiction of the dominion government, we would at once change the original agreement. Would it be fair to assume that a province which has been clothed with exclusive authority in certain matters should now calmly submit to limitation of its powers at the instance of the Senate and House of Commons. Would a province agree to any alteration in regard to its exclusive jurisdiction? I take the view that the provinces should be and must be consulted in regard to any important change in our constitutional act which affects provincial interests. I agree that some constitutional changes are necessary, but I submit that the only way of bringing them about is by agreement between the parties to the original bargain. Of course this statement does not apply to what I discussed a few minutes ago, in regard to matters of form and procedure.

speechtext:
In that case the act was passed with those two or three words added by way of amendment. I agree with the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre that the trend of judicial decisions, particularly the decisions of the judicial committee of the privy council, has in recent years changed considerably. The trend has been entirely towards the enlargement of the powers of the federal government rather than towards restriction of them; notably in the two cases which were decided in 1933 or 1934, the aeronautics case and1 the radio case, cited1 by my hon. friend. Those cases raised the question of the right of the federal parliament to bind the provinces by treaties with foreign countries. In the aeronautics case it was argued that aviation was a provincial matter, at least in some aspects, and that the federal parliament had no power to legislate in respect of it. The question arose under section 132 of the British North America Act which provides that:
The parliament and government of Canada shall have all powers necessary or proper for performing the obligations of Canada or of any province thereof, as part of the British empire, towards foreign countries arising under treaties between the empire and such foreign countries.
It was held in the aeronautics case that the matter of aviation had become of such national importance that it must be placed under dominion control, and that the parliament of Canada, by accepting the international convention in regard to aeronautics, was in a position to bind the provinces under that arrangement.
The radio case was a little different. In that case we had not entered into an international convention to which the British empire was a party. The British empire was not a party to that arrangement. We had entered into a convention with the United States, Mexico, Newfoundland and I think the Irish Free State, agreeing to certain matters concerning radio. We passed an act adopting that convention. That act was challenged, chiefly by the provinces of Quebec and Ontario. The privy council in that case held that radio, like aeronautics, had become a matter of national importance and was under the jurisdiction of the federal authority. They also held that, notwithstanding that the treaty was not one made by the British empire but with foreign countries, it was still within the meaning of section 132 of the British North America Act and that Canada in adopting that treaty by statute was able to bind all the provinces to its terms. These decisions have advanced the matter considerably. I know what the argument of the hon. member for Winnipeg North Center is in respect thereof. Lately we have grown in our national status, and in our national importance; many questions which thirty or forty years ago were not even thought of by our predecessors have now become of great practical importance in this and every other country. I think that one may say that the trend of decisions in the last eight or ten years has been decidedly in favour of some extension of dominion jurisdiction.
My hon. friend quoted a statement by the Prime Minister last session in regard to amendments of the British North America Act, in which the Prime Minister said that there uTere two ways of viewing the matter, one in its strictly legal aspect and the other in what might be called its political aspect. I think the statement of the Prime Minister in the house on that occasion was an exact statement of the situation. Legally this house would have right to pass an address, have it concurred in by the Senate and presented to the imperial parliament. But I do not look on that as a constitutional right. I do not for a moment believe that a request for amendment which interfered with the basis of confederation or with the legislative powers of the provinces would be acceded to by the parliament at Westminster, without the concurrence of the provinces.
B.N.A. Act-Mr. Guthrie

On the other hand there is the political aspect of the case. When these provinces were constituted under the British North America Act they became legal political entities. They are as completely incorporated and authorized as is the parliament of Canada, and unless we can carry their consent and approval in anj matter affecting their exclusive rights I do not think we shall have any chance of securing amendments to our constitutional act from the parliament at Westminster. That is what the Prime Minister meant by the political aspect of the question. There may be a strict legal right but the question is, is it politic, is it wise, is it a right of which we should attempt to avail ourselves. Are all the parties concerned agreeable to it? Such are the questions which would most probably be asked, notwithstanding the strict legal right which my hon. friend has pointed out. My hon. friend must realize that there is a distinction between a legal and a constitutional right.
I do not know, Mr. Speaker, that in my view of this motion it is necessary to enter upon any fuller discussion of the subject. I did note, however, when the leader of the opposition (Mr. Mackenzie King) spoke in this house on Monday last and referred to the question of the amendment of the British North America Act-I am sorry he is not here now-that he made a statement which rather shocked me. I made' a mental and also a written note of it at the time. The right hon. gentleman stated broadly that power should be granted to the parliament of Canada to amend its own constitution. However, after carefully correcting and revising his speech in Hansard, I find that he added some words of limitation. I have seen both the unrevised and the revised copies, and I find that he has added these words:
There ought to be an amendment arrived at as a result of agreement, as I believe it can be.
These words were added after the speech was made. Such is my view of the matter, namely, that an amendment should only be made as the result of an agreement where basic fundamental or important changes are contemplated. I agree that the changes in contemplation outlined by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre in his speech today, are basic. There is the question of the incorporation of companies; there is no doubt that there is serious conflict in that regard. There is the whole question of taxation as between the dominion and the provinces. We in this parliament practically have the right to tax anything and anybody in any manner

we like. We can impose either direct or indirect taxation, while the provinces are limited to direct taxation within the province. I know that in many of the provinces the revenues do not appear to be sufficient to enable them to carry on all their projects at the present time, and I know thait the provinces desire to secure further avenues of taxation if it is possible to secure them.
Then there are many very nice questions which arise under subsection 2 of section 91 of the British North America Act, which provides that this parliament shall have jurisdiction to regulate matters of trade and commerce. That particular section has given rise to more judicial decisions and interpretations than any other section of the acit, and perhaps to as many as all other sections combined. I am glad to say that there has been in recent times a general statement of judicial findings by the judicial committee itself which I think will greatly assist in clarifying a good many points which have hitherto been considerably involved. In the aeronautic case the lord chancellor referred to a case which was decided by the privy council in 1930, known as the Fish Canneries case, he said that the judicial committee had held an inquest in regard to a great many of the decisions of the board, and that it had been found that in the case of the attorney general for Canada against the attorney general for British Columbia, which is the Fish Canneries case, four propositions were stated which in his opinion fairly represented the law on the subject. Those propositions came before the court for decision in the case I have just mentioned, in which a statute was attacked as ultra vires under which the federal government had passed regulations providing among other things that, under certain conditions, all canneries on the Pacific coast should secure licences under the act. In the judgment, delivered in 1929, four specific propositions are laid down; they are not long, and I am going to place them on Hansard:
(1)	The legislation of the parliament of the dominion, so long as it strictly relates to subjects of legislation expressly enumerated in section 91, is of paramount authority, even though it trenches upon matters assigned to the provincial legislatures by section 92.
(2)	The general power of legislation conferred upon the parliament of the dominion by section 91 of the act in supplement of the power to legislate upon the subjects expressly enumerated must be strictly confined to such matters as are unquestionably of national interest and importance, and must not trench on any of the subjects enumerated in section 92 as within the scope of provincial legislation-

B.Nu4. Act-Mr. Lapointe
Note these words:
-unless these matters have attained such dimensions as to affect the body politic of the dominion.
In which event the federal parliament may legislate notwithstanding section 92.
(3)	It is within the competence of the dominion parliament to provide for matters which, though otherwise within the legislative competence of the provincial legislature, are necessarily incidental to effective legislation by the parliament of the dominion upon a subject of legislation expressly enumerated in section 91.
(4)	There can be a domain in which provincial and dominion legislation may overlap, in which case neither legislation will be ultra vires if the field is clear, but if the field is not clear and the two legislations meet the dominion legislation must prevail.
Such was the decision rendered in the British Columbia fish canneries case in 1929, and this decision has been expressly approved as a statement of the present law upon the subject in the aeronautics and radio cases which have been cited this afternoon by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Woodsworth). [DOT]
I agree with my hon. friend that it is high time that some definite step was taken to ascertain if we cannot arrive at some agreement with the provinces in regard to amendments to the British North America Act. I emphasize the word "agreement" because I hold a very strong opinion that we cannot reach any satisfactory conclusion otherwise than by conference and agreement. Therefore I am quite willing to accept this motion on behalf of the government. It has been drawn with the object of safeguarding the rights of minorities in this country. So far as the government is concerned there will be no objection to this motion being adopted and submitted to a select committee of this house.

subtopic: PROPOSAL FOR APPOINTMENT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE TO CONSIDER AMENDMENTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my hon. friend from Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Woodsworth) has raised a most important question, and one which is widely discussed at the present time. As he has stated the act of 1867, though not perfect, Jias been a good instrument of government, but no one will deny that we have developed beyond the rigid limitations of an act which was well adapted to the conditions prevailing sixty-five years ago. At that time there were four colonies, not very thickly populated, and the people in each lived their own lives with very little concern in regard to what was happening in the rest of the country or, for that matter, in the rest of the world.
To-day Canada is a nation, and each part of Canada influences and is influenced by what takes place in the other parts of the country. The conditions of 1867 certainly were not the conditions of to-day. Now we have a line of autonomous provinces extending from ocean to ocean, and the discoveries of science have transformed the existence of the people. Legislatures have to deal with matters which were unthought of at that time. In the early days who would have thought of radio, aviation or even social questions such as old age pensions, unemployment insurance, and workmen's compensation? The result has been that the division of powers between the federal parliament and provincial legislatures has been the cause of interminable litigations and has resulted in much confusion and uncertainty. Constantly appeals are being heard by the privy council regarding the powers of the federal and provincial authorities; sometimes those appeals are at the instance of the dominion government and sometimes at the instance of provincial governments. I may say the honours have been pretty evenly divided. I do not think the privy council has distinguished itself particularly nor has it shown great consistency in its interpretation of the spirit of the British North America Act. As a matter of fact who among the lawyers of this country does not know that when Lord Haldane was one of the powerful members of the board, perhaps the most powerful, there was a leaning towards the provinces. Since Lord Haldane is no longer there and as there are other strong members on the board the trend has been rather on the other side with the result that in later years the federal parliament has been successful. Clearly this condition is undesirable.
Those two subsections of the act which give the most cause for conflict are that part of section 91 assigning to the dominion parliament powers concerning trade and commerce and that part of section 92 giving to the provinces control over matters affecting property and civil rights. The boundary in those two matters is in most cases very hard to discover, and that is the reason there have been so many litigations with regard to the interpretation of the act.
The Lemieux act passed by this parliament in 1907 was enacted to provide that in cases of trouble or conflict between employers and employees they must resort to a conciliation tribunal and that if they do not a strike or lockout is unlawful. If there is a question national in its scope it is the question of the industrial relations between labour and

B.NA. Act-Mr. Lapointe

capital, and if there are strikes throughout the country surely the federal parliament should intervene. On the other side the argument could be urged that troubles are usually caused because of different views concerning hours of labour, contracts between employers and employees and other similar matters which come under that part of section 92 having to do with property and civil rights.
The result was that after operating for about twenty years that piece of legislation passed and enforced by this parliament was challenged in 1926, declared unconstitutional and beyond the powers of this parliament to enact. The same question arises in connection with the insurance problem. No doubt insurance is simply a contract by which a corporation may insure the life or property of the citizen, thereby affecting property and civil rights. On the other hand who will deny that insurance is a matter of national importance? Still, legislation of this parliament concerning insurance has been declared invalid by the privy council.
The two matters to which the Minister of Justice referred, namely radio and aviation, have been decided in favour of this parliament. It is a good thing such decision was made regarding radio, otherwise we might have been prevented from listening to the Prime Minister's reform speeches over the radio. So far as I am concerned that would have been a calamity. The same questions arise when we come to deal with division of revenues between the dominion and the provinces, taxation and other matters.
I believe every person who studies this matter will come to realize the importance of making some changes. What those changes should be, in what manner they should be made and the procedure to adopt before, during and after they are accepted are questions for consideration. I am not one who believes that the constitution, and for that matter the Canadian constitution, is an ark of the covenant which no one may touch or even look at without being guilty of a crime or subject to penalty. In my view the constitution should be adaptable to the changing conditions of a country. I believe no constitutive body, no national assembly meeting for the purpose of establishing a constitution, has any right to prevent future modification of the organism they are creating. I do not believe they have the right to deprive future generations of the competence they themselves have used. If a constitution cannot be changed it is my view that inevitably the change will take place when there is a sufficient trend of 
public opinion, or a great majority in favour of a change. If those changes do not come along the legal and constitutional lines prescribed by law or by the constitution I am afraid they will come because the will of the people ultimately will always prevail. There must be difficulty; there must be ways adopted and fixed which make it very difficult to change the constitution. To make it utterly impossible, I submit, would not be in the interests of the people of the country which is subjected to that constitution.
As far as Canada is concerned let me say that what has been stated is true; I do not know whether it has been stated to-day but I read in Hansard that it was stated last week that Canada is the only dominion in the British commonwealth which does not possess the right to amend its own constitution. Moreover, it is the only federal state in the whole world which has not the power to change its own constitution. The United States, Mexico, Venezuela, Brazil, the Argentine Republic, Australia, Switzerland-all these are federal countries and each of them has a constitution which provides for the way it shall be amended when the necessity arises.
But so far as Canada is concerned, as it is to-day the British North America Act is a statute of the imperial parliament, and there is no mode of amending it prescribed in the act, which means that to amend it another statute is required. There is no room, there is no established practice as to the way in which such an amendment shall be brought about.
Have the provinces the right to be consulted. This is a question that is being discussed. The provinces have been consulted in some cases, but in most cases they have not been. In 1907 when the case of the new allocation of subsidies to provinces was settled, my hon. friend from Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Woodsworth) says that the imperial parliament passed the necessary amendment at that time in spite of the objection of British Columbia. Well, the amendment inserted then did not meet at all the views or wishes of British Columbia. It merely added three words, and did not mean anything. They said in Great Britain at that time that although they were not taking into consideration the objections of Sir Richard McBride, then premier of British Columbia, it did not mean they would always accept the views of the dominion against the provinces if they were not in accord in the future.
However, everybody will agree that the system is uncertain, is vague, is indefinite, and

B.N.A. Act-Mr. Lapointe
is most unsatisfactory. I personally believe that Canada, like all the other autonomous countries in the world, should have the right to amend its own constitution. I believe that an agreement to that effect between all the parties to confederation is not only desirable but possible. I believe that we should take into consideration the various methods of amending as they exist in the constitutions of all the other federal powers and ascertain which would be more adaptable to our own conditions, with the changes which would be necessary to meet our own conditions. Our constitution must be a living instrument capable of being adapted to our national growth, and it is being faithful to the work of Macdonald and Cartier, and the other fathers of confederation to continue their work and see that it receives its full expansion.
Of course, this will be, and I hope my hon. friend from Winnipeg North Centre will agree with me, a most delicate task. It is not so easy as all that. First, what changes should be made in the constitution? Some are desirable, but there are two schools of thought in this country as to that. There are those who are in favour of the strongest concentration or centralized power possible, and who would favour giving to the central power most of the authority which is now subject to provincial jurisdiction. There is another school which believes that there are many matters as to which the will, the customs and the mentality of the different sections of the country in the various provinces should be considered first. For instance, reading the resolution of my hon. friend I see that he mentions only the desirability of giving the dominion government adequate power to deal effectively with urgent economic problems, and so forth. I would like him to have added-and to give to the provinces in their sphere that undoubted authority and jurisdiction which they do not seem to have at the present time. There are many fields in which there is overlapping. In some of these fields it would be better that the authority should be given to the dominion parliament, but do not ask that everything should go to the dominion parliament, as is rather suggested in this resolution. I believe that the powers should be clearly defined and determined, but not necessarily that most of the authority should be given to the central power and less to the provinces. In some fields I believe that the powers of the provinces should be stronger, but this should be determined by making the act clearer and giving it better phraseology.
92582-15*
We must not forget, as the Minister of Justice (Mr. Guthrie) has said, the spirit of the agreement in whatever change takes place. When confederation took place the country was on the verge of civil strife. During the two years which preceded the Quebec conference there had been four successive changes of government. The public men of that time all agreed that they had to get together in order to try to save the country and make it a unit by giving to a central government, authority on all things which were national in their scope, and leaving to the provinces authority on things which should rather be dealt with by the local authorities. The provinces agreed to relinquish some of their powers at the time in favour of the central authority. But no one must forget that after all they did exist before the dominion government existed. These colonies were separate colonies, and they got together. They agreed to relinquish some of their powers, but on the condition that they should be left other powers and that the federal government should never have the right nor the power to interfere within their sphere of jurisdiction. There is another thing I wish to emphasize, and that is that the British North America Act is not only the constitution of this dominion; it is not only the charter of the dominion parliament or of the dominion government; it is just as much a charter of the provinces. It is their constitution as well; it is the law under which they have an existence. My hon. friend said they were a political entity. They are even a legal entity, and I must say that I do not agree with the Prime Minister or with the Minister of Justice when he said that legally this parliament could have the right to change the constitution, the British North America Act, when it comes to matters which are certainly provincial in their scope. I do not agree with that.

speechtext:
Neither legally nor constitutionally could you pass an act providing that property and civil rights belong to the jurisdiction of this parliament. I do not think that can be done, my right hon. friend the Prime Minister to the contrary notwithstanding. And apart from the question concerning minorities there are many other questions which are strictly within the sphere of provincial jurisdiction and should not be taken away from the provinces without agreement with them.
Thirdly, within the limit of its jurisdiction, a provincial legislature is just as autonomous,

B.N.A. Act-Mr. Lapointe
just, as sovereign in the matters on which it has authority to legislate as this parliament is. There is no difference at all in that right of the provincial legislatures and of the dominion parliament. Why, even the statute of Westminster, adopted three years ago, gives this parliament full powers of government; even if the legislation of this parliament comes into conflict with some imperial legislation, it is our legislation that prevails. There is no limitation to the powers of this parliament to enact legislation, even though it is contrary to an imperial statute. Sub-section 2 of section 7 of the Westminster act says:
The provisions of section 2 of this act shall extend to laws made by any of the provinces of Canada and to the powers of the legislatures of such provinces.
This means that tile imperial parliament cannot invalidate a statute of a provincial legislature of Canada legislating within the sphere of its authority. The provincial legislatures are just as autonomous within their jurisdiction as the dominion parliament is.
Now there has been at various times a discussion as to whether the Act of Conledera-tion is a treaty or a pact, and I do not wish to enter into that discussion now. Whether it is a treaty-and it was called such by Sir John Macdonald, by Cartier, by D'Arcy McGee and later on by Sir Robert Borden and Sir Wilfrid Laurier-whether the supporters of the school of thought which now claims that it was not legally a treaty or a pact are right or wrong, I do not wish to discuss. At any rate everyone will agree that it was an understanding, an agreement as between various legislative bodies in North America and that nothing should be done which changes the terms of that agreement without a new understanding, a new consultation, a new conference and, I would add, a new agreement.
I think that a conference with the provinces is a necessary preliminary step to any change which might be made-and, mind you, I am in favour of a change being made. 1 will make this statement now, and I pray you, Mr. Speaker, to believe that it is not my wish to inject anything political into the discussion; I would say the same if the men with whom I sit were on the other side. I do not think that it would be for a dying parliament, just before a general election, to change the constitution of Canada. This question, I think, should be taken up and dealt with by a parliament, a government which is fresh from the people, which has a clear mandate, whatever that government might be. And the same with the provinces.

I think we shall have in the very near future a situation in which almost all the legislatures of Canada will be new. There have been many elections recently, there are new legislatures in most of the provinces, there will be three new provincial elections probably this year, and there will be a federal election. I submit therefore that the time for taking up a question like this would be rather when these legislatures, ours like the others, have a fresh mandate from the people.
I hope that this question will be discussed without any political intent or interest or meaning from whatever side. It would be a disaster if the constitution of Canada, if anything concerning the constitution should become a bone of contention between political parties. I see occasionally suggestions of a national government or a union government being formed for the purpose of settling the railway question or methods of taxation. Well, sir, all these questions are merely questions of administration, and any government can settle them if it has the courage and the strength to do so. If a national government were required -and I am not in favour of it-it would be on a question like this; and I am surprised that those who advocate such a body do not give this as a justification for it. But what I would suggest is this. The conference, as there will have to be one to settle the whole question, instead of being a conference of governments, as the other dominion-provincial conferences have been, ought to be more national in scope, just because it is essential that there should not be any division between parties in this matter. I would suggest that the delegates from the dominion to this convention should be selected as our committees are in the house and should include representatives of all parties in the House of Commons. I would suggest also that the representatives of the legislatures which will meet with the dominion body in order to discuss this most important question ought also to be selected from amongst the various parties in the different legislatures. That would be a really national conference and would eliminate many of the possible troubles and causes of friction which would be very dangerous in this matter.
But hon. members may ask me: What would you suggest as a practical method of amending the constitution? This is what I have already suggested both in this parliament and outside it: when we speak of Canada, we mean Canada as including not only the dominion parliament but the nine provinces as well, and I am in favour of Canada having the right to amend its own constitution; but I would suggest that when an amendment is proposed by this parliament, the change should

B.N.A. Act-Mr. Lachkovich
have to be agreed upon by a majority of two-thirds of the members of the house and the members of the Senate and this change should be submitted to the various provincial legislatures for their approval. On ordinary questions, questions of finance, railways, communication and matters like that, I do not think unanimity ought to be required. It would be an absurdity that one province might on a purely fiscal or financial question, a matter of taxation, prevent the will of the immense majority of the people of Canada from prevailing. A clear majority or a majority of two-thirds of the legislatures might be required on most matters. But on questions of vital importance to some sections of Canada, questions of protection of minorities, the question of school or language, unanimity should be required and I believe the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre has already stated that that is his wish in the matter. That would be the suggestion I would make to a convention representing the dominion and the provinces for discussion. I do not think it is perfect ; it could be improved, but as a subject of discussion it is what I personally would be willing to submit.	_
So far as the resolution of my hon. friend is concerned, of course I have no objection to its being submitted to a committee, but witn that reservation again that it is a little queer that one party to the agreement should study the methods of changing the agreement by itself without inviting the other parties to participate in the discussion.

Mr. Speaker, I am more interested
in the humanity than in the legality of the constitution. Both the hon. member for Quebec East (Mr. Lapointe) and the Minister of Justice (Mr. Guthrie) have spoken of the constitution from the legal aspect. The Minister of Justice said that the constitution of Canada has not within itself the means of amending it. Well, some poet many centuries ago had this to say:
The moving finger writes; and having writ, Moves on; nor all your piety nor wit Shall lure it back to cancel half a line Nor all your tears wash out a word of it.
If that is so, I suppose those hon. members who have tears to shed should prepare to shed them now, because according to the words of the Minister of Justice we, deprived of the ability to amend our own constitution, will not be able to amend it in the near
future. There is a possibility in the same manner as we might tighten the hoops on a barrel so that the barrel might burst, the hoops of the constitution might become so tight on the Canadian people that something in this country might burst. The people have a way of acting like that on occasions.
There is no question of doubt in my mind that this move for constitutional revision is due to the last five years of depression and also to the new philosophy that is at present arising in Canada. The government has launched upon a new political philosophy, claiming that the old order is gone and that we must substitute a new order therefor. Personally I do not feel that we can launch or bring about a ne\v order in Canada until our constitution is changed, because if we try to inaugurate this new order we shall find that so far as the provinces and the dominion are concerned, impediments and obstacles will be placed in the way of constitutional change so as to render it absolutely impossible to make any change in the constitution. Therefore I hold that unless we do change the constitution materially, we shall not be able to inaugurate this new older about which so much is being said, not only in this corner of the house but amongst hon. gentlemen opposite. The people throughout the country ten years ago were not interested in constitutional changes; all they were interested in was a job, and having a job few of them were interested in the constitution at all. It was not until 1929 when the depression and the crisis began that the people at large commenced to think seriously about the constitution by which this country is governed. We have been told in the schools about the infallibility and immutability of the constitution and speakers at various picnics have told us about the supreme wisdom of the fathers of confederation. But people are beginning to doubt that supreme wisdom and at the present time it is very difficult to get a speaker at those picnics and other festive occasions to speak so eulogistically of the men who drafted our constitution. The constitution was a product of the economic philosophy of the times; the laissez-faire philosophy, then in its hey-day. But times have changed since 1867; we now have a new economic philosophy which is held not only by this group and others in the house and throughout the country but to which even the Prime Minister has become a convert. It has been said that we would meet with difficulties in regard to provincial jurisdiction. I have in my hand a report of the case of Snyder v

B.NA. Act-Mr. Luchkovich
Toronto Electric Commissioners, in which the province denied the validity of dominion legislation providing for compulsory investigation of labour disputes in public utilities, and it was discovered that the dominion had not the power to implement the signatures of its representatives to the international convention for the eight-hour day.
Suggestions have been asked for. Take the matter of social services, regulation of wages and hours of labour; why can this not be under the control of the federal authorities rather than have the situation that exists today in which we are faced with provincial impediments at every step? I asked an unemployed man the other day what he thought about these attacks on the constitution and on liberty, and this is what he said: So far as those sections of the constitution that are absolutely necessary to safeguard certain necessary rights in this country are concerned the constitution should be upheld, but if it is being used merely as a cloak for some ulterior motive or to prevent essential legislation then I say the constitution should be radically changed. Can you imagine any leader in this country haranguing a crowd of unemployed men and women about the benefits of liberty and the constitution and the dangers of losing both when all the while they are thinking about the condition in which they now find themselves of misery and demoralizing idleness and starvation in the midst of plenty? These are the things about which people are thinking at the present time. They feel that they have been circumscribed by a sort of economic straight-jacket from which they are finding it very hard to extricate themselves.
I have said that the constitution as drafted in 1867 is a reflection of the economic thought of the times. The constitution in 1935 should be a reflection of the economic conditions that now exist. If we are to launch this new order, call it government intervention if you wilf I do not think it has much chance of success unless the constitution is radically amended to suit the new order. Let the constitution fit the times and the needs of the people rather than have the people fit arbitrarily into the constitution.
Motion agreed to.

No suggestion is made that some encouragement be given to these yards, to build our own ships, to keep our own artisans at work. This

I anticipated before the
house rose at six o'clock that some question might be raised as to the calling of the motion standing in the name of the hon. member for West Middlesex (Mr. Elliott), so I took the opportunity during recess of looking up one or two authorities. I must confess that the matter is not without some doubt. At the same time the authorities are fairly clear to the effect that the motion standing in the name of the hon. member for West Middlesex is out of order under the anticipation rule. I should first like to quote from Campion, Introduction to the Procedure of the House of Commons, page 152, under the heading Anticipation in Debate. Before referring to the paragraph which I shall quote, let me say that I do not think there can be any question of doubt as to the similarity of material in the two motions, that standing in the name of Mr. Elliott, and the one which subsequently appears on the order paper. To quote from Campion:
The anticipation rule, which forbids discussion on a matter standing on the paper being forestalled, is dependent on the same principle as that which forbids the same question being twice raised in the same session. In applying the anticipation rule preference is given to the discussion-
And I think emphasis might be placed on the following words:
-which lead's to the most effective result.
To continue:
And this has established a descending scale of values for discussions-bills, motions, amendments, etc. Thus a bill or other order of the day must not be anticipated by (or more shortly
IMr. I. A. Mackenzie.]
blocks) discussion of a motion, amendment, or subject raised on another motion, such as that for the adjournment of the house. A motion standing on the paper for leave to bring in a bill blocks discussion of a motion (except for the presentation of a bill), amendments, etc. Any substantive motion standing on the paper blocks the discussion of an amendment, etc. An amendment on the paper blocks the raising of its subject in debate.
Frankly, one question rather worried me, as to what "bill" meant in Campion. In order to follow that up somewhat I find a precedent in May to this effect-see 341 House Debates, 35-762:
The fact that a bill has not been printed does not withdraw it from the operation of this rule.
The Speaker's ruling on that occasion was as follows:
The hon. member cannot move the amendment which stands in his name because it raises a discussion of a bill of which notice has already been given by the government.
I take it that the item appearing on the order paper under the head of Government Notices of Motions, standing in the name of the Minister of Finance, is tantamount to a notice such as is referred to in the authority which I have just given. I take it that the word "bill" in Campion is used in the widest sense, embracing the various steps through which a bill must pass before it is finally approved by this house. The first step taken in connection with the bill under consideration is the step set out on the order paper. With the very greatest deference to the opinions which have been expressed to the contrary, I rule that the motion standing in the name of the hon. member for West Middlesex is out of order.

speechtext:
Whereas, the attention of this house has been drawn by the royal commission to inquire into railways and transportation in Canada to the urgent necessity which exists for an early consideration of the capital structure of the Canadian railways (section 84-87 of that report):
And whereas, that commission recognized that a very substantial part pf the money invested in the railways comprised within the Canadian National Railway system must be regarded as lost, and that its capital liabilities should be heavily written down, although the said royal commission did not deem the time opportune when making the said report to deal with this important matter, but suggested that the same receive early consideration by the board of trustees;
And whereas, a board of trustees has been appointed by the government;
Therefore be it resolved, that in the opinion of this house, it is of vital importance that the attention of the board of trustees of the Canadian National Railways be directed to this matter, and that this house deems it highly desirable that the said board of trustees shall consider this question and report thereon with the least possible delay as being of vital and primary importance in the interests of all concerned.
He said: Mr. Speaker, this resolution speaks for itself. I introduced this question during the session of 1934; there was very little debate and eventually it died on the order paper. This year I should like to have this matter discussed by hon. members generally. Every year we have this matter of the deficit of the Canadian National Railways thrown
up to us, and it is not fair. It is not fair to the people of Canada or to the employees of the system. The money has been lost; the capital assets should be written down. You could easily write off perhaps a billion dollars, and charge it to profit and loss where it belongs. If you did that even to-day the Canadian National Railways would be able to carry its load.
We have a similar case in British Columbia; we have a little railroad with which most hon. members are familiar. I refer to the Pacific Great Eastern railway. To-day the capital structure of that railway is 874,000,000. I have been over every foot of the line; I know the country well, and I estimate the replacement value at possibly 820,000,000. Why should the capital be continued at 874,000,000 when it is worth only 820,000,000, or 825,000,000? If that were written down even that road would pay its way. So I say that in all fairness to the people of Canada, to the shippers, to the employees and to everyone else, this question should be considered very seriously.
This is a big question. Our railways represent the greatest financial problem we must face to-day, and I plead with hon. members of the house to discuss the matter. Let us hear from other hon. members. This is a reasonable business proposition. I am not introducing the matter from any political motive; I am doing so in fairness to the Canadian National Railways.
I need not take up the time of the house at any greater length, but I should like hon. members to pay some attention to and consider this matter for a short time. I may be all wrong in my views; if I am I should like to have it pointed out to me. I still say, however, that if the capital were written down a billion dollars or more there would be no deficit on the Canadian National. I am speaking of the railways, not of the hotels or steamship lines. I plead earnestly with hon. members to say whether I am right or wrong in my argument.
