There seems to be so much misinformation in regard to this whole question. If I understood my hon. friend aright he suggested that if we recapitalized the Canadian National railways, writing down the capital by a thousand million dollars, in some way or other we might avoid the yearly deficit.
C.N'.R.-Capital Structure

subtopic: PROPOSED CONSIDERATION OF CAPITAL STRUCTURE BY BOARD OF TRUSTEES
speechtext: Set up the capital structure to measure up with your assets.

subtopic: PROPOSED CONSIDERATION OF CAPITAL STRUCTURE BY BOARD OF TRUSTEES
speechtext: If we set up the capital structure of the Canadian National Railways to-day so as to measure up to our earnings we would not only have to wipe out a thousand million dollars-

subtopic: PROPOSED CONSIDERATION OF CAPITAL STRUCTURE BY BOARD OF TRUSTEES
speechtext: I did not say that; I said your assets.

subtopic: PROPOSED CONSIDERATION OF CAPITAL STRUCTURE BY BOARD OF TRUSTEES
speechtext: The physical value.

subtopic: PROPOSED CONSIDERATION OF CAPITAL STRUCTURE BY BOARD OF TRUSTEES
speechtext:
Perhaps I might finish my sentence. If we set up the assets of the Canadian National railways in such a way as to be proportionate at all with the earnings today we would have to wipe out a thousand million dollars owing to the government, plus another four hundred million dollars carried on the books of the company as owing to the government, plus practically the whole of the
SI,255,000,000 owing to the public investors of the country. It is true that there was a time, in 1928, the peak year, when the Canadian National Railways did earn sufficient to pay the interest of that day. During that year, when world business was booming, the Canadian National did a gross business of $304,000,000, and the net, in other words the profit available for interest amounted to $44,000,000. In other words the sum of $44,000,000 could go towards the payment of interest, and as the interest in 1928 amounted to $41,000,000, in that year the Canadian National railways bad a profit, over and above the payment of interest, of $3,000,000. That and one other year, namely 1926, were the only two years in which the Canadian National Railways earned sufficient to pay the interest in the corresponding year. But it must be pointed out that while in 1928 the Canadian National system earned sufficient to pay the interest at that day, which was $41,000,000, it was vastly too little-if I may use what may appear to be a contradiction in terms- to have paid the interest of to-day, because the interest of to-day owing to the public- and this has nothing to do with the interest owing to the government-instead of being $41,000,000 as it was in 1928 is in fact $57,000,000. So it is obvious that even if the Canadian National Railways had obtained in 1934 the volume of business it had in 1928, or if it had the same net earnings, or the same amount to apply on interest, it would still be $16,000,000 short of paying the interest.
I point that out first so that hon. members may understand the situation. I am not arguing against the trustees dealing with this matter, but there has been so much misinformation and misunderstanding concerning
 -
the whole problem that I shall endeavour during a few moments this evening to explain the situation as clearly as I can. I do this more for the public than for the house because I am quite sure every hon. member understands the situation thoroughly. However there is a great deal of misunderstanding outside this chamber. For instance quite recently I received a letter from a gentleman suggesting that if we would cut the interest on Canadian National Railway bonds owing to the public from six per cent to a reasonable figure we would save an amount sufficient to pay the deficit on the railway system. Well, his first mistake is that the average interest is not six per cent; in 1934 it was exactly 4i per cent. He was wrong from that angle. Again and again I see the statement in letters appearing in the newspapers, and sometimes in editorial comments, that if we would recapitalize the Canadian National system by wiping out the government debt we would be putting the Canadian National in a position to carry itself. I repeat that we would have to wipe out the whole government debt, and then we would not get the desired result because the government debt has been accumulating for years. Never in all the years the Canadian National Railways have been in existence has one cent of that government debt been paid off or one cent of the interest on the government debt been paid to the government by the railways. So that even if we wiped out the whole $1,490,000,000, the amount which the Canadian National bocks show as owing by the railways to the government.-I repeat, if we wiped out that sum, amounting to nearly a billion and a half dollars, and if we eliminated it for all time from the books of the Canadian National Railways, it would have no effect whatsoever upon those railways as a going concern. We would still have exactly the same amount of interest to pay to the public who have invested their money-millions of dollars of it -in the bonds of the Canadian National Railways.
In other words there are two debts owing by the Canadian National Railways. First there is the debt about which I have been speaking, namely the one owing to the government and amounting to $1,490,000,000 including interest and other charges. May I say that it is debatable whether or not some of those charges should be charged against the railways, but the fact is they do appear on the books of the company. We must remember that more than half of the $1,490,000,000 owing to the government went into the building of the Canadian National railways as they

C.NJI.-Capital Structure
stand to-day. For example, it went into the building of the Intercolonial railway; it went into the building of the Prince Edward Island railway; it went into the building of the National Transcontinental railway, and it went into additions and betterments of various other branches which the Canadian National system took over at various times throughout the years under different governments. That is the debt upon which, as I have said, nothing has ever been returned to the government either in capital expenditure or in interest. So that has never been anything but a bookkeeping charge against the Canadian National Railway. To-day the interest upon the debt upon which interest is charged amounts to something over $30,000,000 per annum, but it is only a bookkeeping entry and it has never been paid. I want that clearly understood.

subtopic: PROPOSED CONSIDERATION OF CAPITAL STRUCTURE BY BOARD OF TRUSTEES
speechtext: But it is very often quoted.

subtopic: PROPOSED CONSIDERATION OF CAPITAL STRUCTURE BY BOARD OF TRUSTEES
speechtext: Yes, it is often quoted, but I doubt if the quoting does any particular damage to the railway.

subtopic: PROPOSED CONSIDERATION OF CAPITAL STRUCTURE BY BOARD OF TRUSTEES
speechtext: It does not do any good.

subtopic: PROPOSED CONSIDERATION OF CAPITAL STRUCTURE BY BOARD OF TRUSTEES
speechtext:
It does not do any good, but it is true. I do not know that there can be any advantage in hiding an absolute truth, and I do not think the Canadian National system would be better off from having hidden something from the people of the country.
May I interject that to-day the railways are to my mind efficiently and economically handled, and I do not think they would be any more efficiently and economically handled if that figure were wiped off the books of the company. I do not think that feature has ever made an atom of difference in the handling of the railways either in the past or in the present. It is merely a bookkeeping entry and keeps the picture straight, so far as that figure of $1,490,000,000 is concerned. Some of the charges I think might well be wiped out without doing any damage; anybody will know that some of the charges should not be considered.
The other debt-and this is the debt which counts-is the long term debt owing to the public amounting to $1,255,000,000. That amount is owing to the bondholders in England, the United States and Canada. A large proportion of the bonds, probably from seventy-five to eighty-five per cent, are guaranteed by the people of this dominion, and the only way by which the $57,000,000 of interest upon those bonds can be lowered is by refunding, as is being done from time to 92582-16
time, or by repudiation. The government of Canada is the guarantor of those bonds, and in addition the bonds are a mortgage upon the lines of railway in the Canadian National system. That is really the only debt which counts, namely the debt owing to the investing bondholders. I should like to have that point clear, and, as I have stated, I make it for people outside this chamber rather than hon. members. By no method of bookkeeping could any part of that $57,000,000 of interest, the part which makes the real deficit, be wiped out, except by absorption into the consolidated debt of the Dominion of Canada. That is the only way it could be done. In other words to have an effect to the extent of one cent upon the Canadian National railways one would not only have to wipe out the first debt which I have mentioned, the government debt, and absorb it as most of it has already been absorbed into the national debt of Canada, but in addition one would have to wipe out part of the debt of $1,255,000,000 which is owing to the bondholders in various parts of the world.

subtopic: PROPOSED CONSIDERATION OF CAPITAL STRUCTURE BY BOARD OF TRUSTEES
speechtext: What objection would you have to that?

subtopic: PROPOSED CONSIDERATION OF CAPITAL STRUCTURE BY BOARD OF TRUSTEES
speechtext:
I do not know that I have any particular objection, but I shall give reasons why I think the hon. member's resolution is at least to some degree hasty. I do not use that term offensively, but if the hon. member will permit I will endeavour to explain what I mean. I am endeavouring simply to make clear in the public mind the financial position of the railways.
At this point may I emphasize another fact. Sometimes the statement is made by hon. members and sometimes by the public generally that if we could wipe out or recapitalize the Canadian National Railways-and I must observe that what is meant by recapitalization is not clear-we could improve the situation of the employees, the shippers and the federal situation generally. I think hon. members will understand that those points are not really affected by the bookkeeping entry which has existed for years. We must remember that after all we should have a set-up before the minds of the Canadian people concerning the cost of railways in general and the Canadian National Railways in particular. There is no reason why we should hide the facts. If we did hide the facts there would be the disadvantage that once again we would have the probability of all governments, if you like, and all parties forgetting the errors of the past and encouraging greater expenditures of one kind and another. There is this to remember, that in that government debt there are entries which to my

C.N.R.-Capital Structure

mind will ultimately have to be wiped out and so far as that goes I agree with my hon. friend. For example, the Intercolonial railway was not built as a financial proposition at all; it was built for national and intra-empire reasons. It was built for the sake of rounding out confederation, linking up Halifax and the east with central Canada, and therefore something must be charged up to the country generally of that cost of the Intercolonial railway which is included in the debt owing to the government. Then there was the transcontinental railway and various branch lines that were built. Some of them were built for colonization purposes, some to assist settlers in various parts of Canada, just as my hon. friend from Peace River (Mr. Kennedy) urges at the present time that we should build an outlet from the Peace River section to the coast, even if it did not pay its way, in order to serve the people who are living in that very fine but rather far-off section of Canada.
Then again we bought various railway lines which became a charge upon the Canadian National Railway and, through the Canadian National Railway upon the Dominion of Canada. The purchase of some of these lines was certainly brought about by political and public pressure. Certain sections of the country, in fact nearly all sections that had small railway lines, pressed sufficiently hard to get the government or the Canadian National to absorb those lines into the Canadian National system, and so far as public pressure and political pressure was responsible for that result and thereby laid a charge on the Canadian National Railway just so far should a certain amount of that cost ultimately be absorbed into the public debt of Canada. I am giving my own viewpoint at the moment.
In conclusion, I would point out that according to the report of the Duff commission what my hon. friend seeks by his resolution has already been carried out because the Duff commission in their report, speaking of the financial set-up, said:
This question as well as that previously referred to, dealing with the present involved financial structure of the Canadian National system, should, in the opinion of the commission, have the early attention of the board of trustees, which it is recommended should be entrusted with the control and management of ihe system.
Therefore since the board of trustees was appointed just a little over a year ago it is obvious, if they are carrying out their duties, and I presume they are, that they are studying this question, and as soon as they feel capable of submitting a report upon it through the railway committee to the House of Commons

they will submit that report. I do not think anything is being lost by waiting or that anything is to be gained by haste in this matter. I believe we might well allow the board of trustees as at present constituted to study the whole question thoroughly and submit their report, as soon as they have come to a conclusion upon the matter, and then the House of Commons will be able to deal with the whole question.
In the meantime I suggest to my hon. friend that having brought this question before the House of Commons, and having submitted his reasons for thinking that a little greater haste should be made by the board of trustees than is being made, he might be willing to withdraw his resolution because to my mind there is nothing to be gained by passing it, and on the other hand I think there is something to be gained by allowing the board of trustees, who have many important questions to deal with to take their time in studying what my hon. friend calls this very vital question and making their submissions upon it. I would therefore again suggest to him that he withdraw his resolution after whatever discussion may take place upon it in the house, and I assure him that the resolution will be drawn to the attention of the board of trustees who, I have no doubt, will in the near future make a report on the question to the House of Commons.

speechtext: Although I have no direct information regarding it, I have no doubt they are. subtopic: PROPOSED CONSIDERATION OF CAPITAL STRUCTURE BY BOARD OF TRUSTEES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, with most of what
the Minister of Railways (Mr. Manion) has

submitted to the house I can express myself in agreement because everything he has said has been a reason why this rewriting of the financial structure or revaluation should be carried out.
The minister gave as his only reason why we should not act on this resolution at the present time the fact that instructions were given to the board of trustees by the report of the Duff commission that they should investigate this question and make a recommendation to parliament. But I would suggest to the minister that he note the particular terms of the resolution, which asks "that the attention of the board of trustees of the Canadian National Railways be directed to this matter." That is what the resolution of the hon. member for Vancouver North (Mr. Munn) asks, that this house should draw the attention of the board of trustees of the Canadian National Railways to the matter. That has already been suggested by the Duff commission. The hon. member for Vancouver North thinks it is a matter of vital importance. I agree with him in that respect, and by his remarks to-night the minister shows that he also agrees with him in that respect.
The minister has pointed to the fictitious valuation of the Canadian National Railways as carried on the books of the railway company. That fictitious valuation lends itself day after day throughout Canada to misrepresentation either by those who are opposed to the public owmership of the railway or by those who are anxious to show that the Canadian National Railway is doing worse than it is actually doing, or that the Canadian Pacific Railway is suffering under a great handicap by virtue of the competition of this publicly owned railway. All of these things may be true, but I suggest that the railway has an actual value. It is probably not the value of what we owe outside, not the value of the bonded indebtedness, of what is owing to the Canadian people; it is probably more than that; it may be less, but it has an actual value of some kind, and that valuation cannot be based on its earnings as the minister suggested might possibly be done. If the industries of Canada were to have their valuation based on their earnings to-day there would be very little value in many of them. For that reason I suggest seriously to the minister that he do not ask the hon. member for Vancouver North to withdraw his resolution. We are asking the board of trustees, as trustees for the Canadian people, to place the property on a 92582-164
proper valuation, so that we can accurately visualize what is taking place year by year, instead of maintaining a valuation w'hich we all know to be fictitious. We can get no exact information so long as we maintain this fictitious valuation and so long as we are told that the deficits of hundreds of millions are bookkeeping entries. Let us get away from these bookkeeping entries and get down to business.

Not as a direct charge against the Intercolonial railway; it has not been a charge in the way the minister says. Now I wish to protest, if it is not too late, even if I appear to have been derelict in my duty in the past, when a minister of the crown, and even if it appears that the Duncan commission did not discover that item to be a charge in the way suggested-I wish to protest, I say, when the maritimes are now laying their case before a royal commission appointed by this government, against any charge being made against the Intercolonial railway by the federal government as a debt due to the federal government for the construction of that road. We came into confederation at the call and the request of Ontario and Quebec. We were doing very well by ourselves before we came into confederation-and I am not opposed to confederation, as I said once before. No matter what we think it may have brought us, I for one am still a warm supporter of confederation. But let me say to the house and to the Minister of Railways that long before Ontario and Quebec knew what railway construction-was, we in the maritimes were building railways for our own business; and under the terms of confederation we handed over those railways to the federal government to help Ontario and Quebec. They told us at that time that they had no Atlantic outlet; that they were at the behest of the United States lines; that the United States lines had a monopoly and that they had to transfer their freight from the old country to the United States railroads. In order to show their loyalty to the old country they appealed to our loyalty to come into a confederation
and if we did so they would guarantee construction of the Intercolonial railway from Levis down to Halifax, taking in at that time what they called the old eastern extension and other roads running from Shediac to Saint John, from Saint John to Moncton, from Truro to Halifax and, although I may be in error in this, from Truro to Pictou Landing. Only for administrative purposes. In 1919 an order in council was passed in which it was stated that the directors of the Canadian National Railways as then organized would be the administrators of the old Intercolonial railway. The accounts of the old Intercolonial railway, if not from Montreal down through Levis and on to Halifax, at least from Levis before the Drummond road was taken in as an extension of the old Intercolonial-at least from Levis to Halifax, Sydney and New Glasgow-are kept separate and apart; they are not in the general accounts of the Canadian National Railways at all. That is the reason why in the question I put on the order paper I asked for information so that I and other members from the maritimes might be in a position to burl back into their faces the statement of those who say that the Intercolonial has been a sinkhole in the past. I wish to have that information and I am told that it will be brought down, not by the ordinary method but by a return. When shall I get that return
C.NJt.-Capital Structure

in order to defend the position of the old Intercolonial? I wish to hurl back their statement into the faces of those, especially from Ontario, who say, for the purpose of effecting an amalgamation of the Canadian Pacific and the Canadian National, that the Intercolonial has been a sinkhole. I want to show by this information that the Intercolonial had surplus upon surplus year after year. In some years there were deficits. I remember that when the old Intercolonial railway was the most prosperous, freight rates were the lowest. It was not until 1912 that the agreement under which we came into confederation was departed from when, the late Hon. Frank Cochrane, then Minister of Railways, increased the freights on the old Intercolonial railway to make them correspond with all the freight rates west of Montreal. After the Grand Trunk Pacific passed down through the province, it is true that freight from the northern section was in many cases diverted from the old Intercolonial railway and in that way deficits did occur. If hon. members will examine the record of what is known as the Atlantic region of the present Canadian National railway system, what will they find? They will find that within the last two years, whatever increase there has been in carloadings the greater majority has been over the Atlantic region of the Canadian National, which is the old Intercolonial. To think we, down in the maritimes, have to stand the brunt of the arguments advanced by members from the two old provinces that dragged us into confederation, when they say that we gave Canada a railroad that is nothing but a sinkhole!
Let me draw the attention of the house to the further fact that the old Intercolonial railway is 225 or 250 miles longer to-day than was anticipated when the fathers of confederation asked the maritimes to come into this association. It was not the will of the maritime provinces that brought about the difference in length of that railway. We were forced to go down by the northern route instead of down the valley of Saint John and across close to the northern section of the state of Maine. The imperial government interfered and for the sake of military strategy they said to the confederation at that time, that is, Ontario, Quebec and the two maritime provinces, Nova Scotia and New Brunswick: We desire that this line shall be built such and such a distance from the United States border in case of trouble with the United States so that our railroad will be safeguarded by distance. The imperial government, in order to induce us to do this, paid a con-

tribution of I forget how many million pounds to aid in the construction of the old Intercolonial railway. It is a wonder to me that those who are instrumental in making that charge an amount due to the government by the old Intercolonial railway did not make that payment or contribution of the home government a charge against the Intercolonial as well. Indeed, that may have been done; I am not too sure that it has not. It may be worth while looking into the matter before we get through with this question.
A great deal more could be said in connection with this railway matter but I am going to defer any more remarks I have to make until I have received the information for which I have asked.
Mr. JEAN-FRANCOIS POULIOT (Temis-couata):	This is indeed one of the least
contentious motions that has ever been submitted to the House of Commons. The hon. member for Vancouver North (Mr. Munn) does not ask the house to define or state any policy; he only expresses the wish that the house submit a certain matter to the trustees of the Canadian National Railways; that is all we find in this resolution. The first paragraph contains a statement of fact. It reads thus:
Whereas, the attention of this house has been drawn by the royal commission to inquire into railways and transportation in Canada to the urgent necessity which exists for an early consideration of the capital structure of the Canadian railways (section 84-87 of that report):
This nobody can deny. It is a statement of fact, and that fact is admitted.
And whereas, that commission recognized that a very substantial part of the money invested in the railways comprised within the Canadian National railway system must be regarded as lost, and that its capital liabilities should be heavily written down, although the said royal commission did not deem the time opportune when making the said report to deal with this important matter, but suggested that the same receive early consideration by the board of trustees;
That also was expressed by the royal commission. The royal commission did a certain work, but that work was not complete, especially in regard to labour. If I am not mistaken there was only one paragraph of that report which related to the relations between labour and the company. It was most incomplete. But as the commissioners could not complete their work they directed the attention of the House of Commons to the very fact mentioned in this paragraph. By bringing the matter to the attention of the house the hon. member for Vancouver North
JANUARY 28, 193a	247
C.N.R.-Capital Structure
tries to have the commission's work completed by the trustees who are now in charge of the railway's business.
The third paragraph is:
And whereas, a board of trustees has been appointed by the government;
This is also a statement of fact which cannot be denied. Then the conclusion is:
Therefore be it resolved, that, in the opinion of this house, it is of vital importance that the attention of the board of trustees of the Canadian National Railways be directed to this matter, and that this house deems it highly desirable that the said board of trustees shall consider this question and report thereon with the least possible delay as being of vital and primary importance in the interests of all concerned.
In this house we have to be informed of facts. It is impossible for any member of parliament to read all the bluebooks thoroughly. We have officials in various spheres who are supposed to do that. For this railway system there are three trustees, who have been honoured with the confidence of the crown and about whom I have nothing to say at present, except that I have got in touch with Mr. Labelle and I was well satisfied with the way I was answered when I wrote to him. What we need here in the House of Commons is full information about the basic facts, then we may draw our own conclusions. A moment ago there was a little discussion between the Minister of Railways (Mr. Manion) and the hon. member for Gloucester (Mr. Veniot). They were approaching the matter from different points of view and were not agreeing about the facts. One or other of them is right, but I cannot say which. It is most important to have the facts brought before us from the trustees, and it is most important that their attention should be .brought to the matter in order that they, with the experience that they have acquired in that business by dealing with it for a few years, should make that study for us. They would draw their conclusions, but at the same time we should have the facts upon which those conclusions were based, and this house would have opportunity afterwards to form its own judgment on the matter.
The hon. member for Vancouver North is not now asking the government to change its policy in regard to the Canadian National Railways. Often the Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett) himself has said that Canada has reached the limit of her credit. It has been stated here in Ottawa and elsewhere. We have to know everything about the capital structure of the Canadian National Railways.
I shall not repeat what has been said by other members, but it is most important for us to have a report about that matter at the earliest date possible. In what has been said by the Minister of Railways there is nothing in opposition to this resolution. He cannot say anything against it. The government would not be compromised by accepting it. It would not change the policy of the government at all. It is just asking for a report by the persons best qualified to study the whole matter and to report to us. After that report reaches us the government will be able to state their policy in the matter, when they have full information. That is why I congratulate the hon. member for Vancouver North upon having brought this resolution before the house.
There are some complaints about the Canadian National Railways being unable to meet their liabilities. Some of the interest is on bonds held by the government. The government knows very well that it will take a very long time to pay them. On the other hand the Prime Minister and some of his colleagues often speak about the inability of the Canadian National Railways to meet their liabilities just on account of the interest that is due to the government on those bonds. Therefore I do not see how any member of this house should object to getting good, reliable information on a matter of such vital interest.

I oppose the resolution for one reason; that it is calculated to make us forget how foolish we have been in years past. That I think is something we should not forget. Neither do I think we should do anything that would tend to that end.
As far as the remarks of the hon. member for Gloucester (Mr. Veniot) are concerned, to a very large extent I am in sympathy with the position he takes. There is no question that the mileage of the Intercolonial was needlessly increased by at least three hundred to four hundred miles simply from a military point of view, at the instance of the British government of that day. It is a mistake to suppose that all the branch lines in the maritime provinces were unprofitable. For instance one branch line taken over was in my own county of Pictou. It was some twelve and a half miles long. That road always paid a small return on the capital; it paid the larger amount during the summer months, while in most winters there was a slight loss due to difference in traffic. And there were other roads in the maritime provinces that were earning money.
C.NJI.-Capital Structure

It is not my intention to discuss this matter at any length, but I repeat that I am opposed to the resolution simply for the reason that I think it is a mistake to do anything to remove from our minds and memories the colossal mistakes we made in this country in regard to railway construction. That loaded us with a debt that neither our children nor our grandchildren will see wiped out. There is no way to wipe it out; we have to pay the interest, and no matter of bookkeeping is going to alter that unfortunate fact. A good many of us would like to forget some other mistakes we made in the last four or five years. It would not help us one iota if we could erase from memory's pages many of the mistakes we made in 1928 and 1929. It is well that we should remember them and profit by them, and the same thought applies to the question of the capitalization of the Canadian National railways.

maintopic: SUPPLY-REFORM MEASURES AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF THE MINISTER OF JUSTICE FOR COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY

speechtext: Hon. HUGH GUTHRIE (Minister of Justice) moved that the house go into committee of supply.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Leader of the Opposition):
maintopic: SUPPLY-REFORM MEASURES AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF THE MINISTER OF JUSTICE FOR COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, no doubt your honour will remember that when the debate on the address took place I offered cooperation with the government on the part of the official opposition in connection with the consideration of all measures having to do with the pressing question of unemployment, as well as those measures of social and industrial reform which we were advised would be the main concern of this parliament at its present session, but I pointed out that as the time of this parliament might be distinctly limited, since the government had it within its power at any moment to bring on a general election before measures of industrial and social reform were properly considered, it would be advisable that those measures should be brought down at the earliest possible moment, and that the time of parliament should not meanwhile be devoted to less important business.
In order that the government might have every opportunity to bring down its legislation at an early date and in as complete a form as possible I said that I would ask hon. members on this side to refrain from participating in the debate on the address, and would seek to have the speeches of the opposition confined to the speech which might be made by myself. Hon. members on this side acted in accordance with that suggestion, and to a certain extent hon. members in other parts of the house restricted the number of their speeches. There were a few speeches by hon. members of the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation, speeches by the independent members, and a few from the government side. Debate on the address was thus brought to a speedy conclusion, and I believe all hon

Reform Measures-Mr. Mackenzie King
members then hoped and thought the way was clear for the consideration, or at least the introduction, of some of the measures of social and industrial reform which we have been called to consider.
I made a further suggestion respecting private members' motions to the effect that with the consent of the house we might forego the consideration of such measures at the present time and if need be consider them later. I was careful to point out that no hon. member should be deprived of his right to speak on any motion he might have on the order paper. I suggested such an arrangement would have to have unanimous consent, and I believe it would have received such consent had not the Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett) indicated that he did not purpose changing the order of procedure and would not put any motion of the kind. For that reason we have had to consider private members' motions. However hon. members on this side of the house have adopted a self-denying ordinance and have foregone any lengthy discussion or all discussion of the motions appearing in the names of hon. members of the opposition. We have been content to allow other hon. members to indicate their points of view and to indicate ours simply by taking such action as might be necessary to indicate our support or disapproval.
The house has now gone completely through private members' motions. Every number on the order paper has been called and several of the motions have been discussed. A few have been passed by deliberately in order to give the government an opportunity to bring on its measures of social reform. For example I would point to the motion respecting titles standing in my name. I attach a good deal of importance to the discussion of that subject but I have felt that if the motion came before the house a somewhat lengthy debate might be created, that a considerable amount of time might be necessary for discussion and, as a consequence, in case I might be absent when it was called, I asked the hon. member for Quebec East (Mr. Lapointe) to inform the chair of my desire to have it stand for the present in order that the house might proceed more quickly with those measures about which the people of the country are very greatly concerned. That was done.
My third suggestion was that if we could proceed with the program of social and industrial reform, with the measures concerning social insurance and with the reform of the capitalistic system I would undertake, so far as supply was concerned, to state on behalf of the opposition that we would have little difficulty in reaching an agreement with the government regarding the voting of supply at a later time. I am now again prepared to give that undertaking. I have looked through the estimates, and with the exception of some of the items in the different departments I think we could agree to their passage. We may find it necessary to discuss some votes where salaries have been considerably increased, but other than that I believe we could agree to pass the civil supply very quickly, once we have had before us all the social and industrial reform measures. As hon. members are aware however, once the house resolves itself into committee of supply, debate may be protracted to any length; supply may be brought up day after day, and we may be kept here doing little more than considering supply one day after another. That is a means governments sometimes take to fill in time when they are not ready with more important legislation.
We have been told by the Prime Minister that the social reform legislation is so allimportant that no time must be lost. He has said we must proceed with it with haste. Not only have we been told that but the people of Canada were told the same thing over the radio before parliament assembled. They were told that in part at least they would see the program outlined in the speech from the throne and that the government would go on with the work immediately. In these circumstances-

The hon. member has asked when the word "immediately" was used. If he wishes to quibble over a word I shall withdraw the word "immediately" altogether. I will give him the Prime Minister's own words. I believe he did not use the word "immediately" but he did use the word "now," and the expression "as quickly as possible." Further he used the expression "go on without delay," the further expression "speed and determination," and the expression "not any other time, but right now." If I used the word "immediately" as comprehending the lot or synonomous with each I hope exception will not be taken.
When a week ago to-day the Prime Minister introduced the resolution standing on the order paper respecting social insurance he said he was doing so so that "to-morrow" the resolution might be considered.

speechtext: That is a form.

speechtext:
Yes, but the word "to-morrow" means that the matter may be discussed at the earliest possible moment

Reform Measures[DOT]-Mr. Mackenzie King
in the order of procedure in which it appears on the order paper. For that reason I do not think I am far wrong when I state the impression left upon the house and country *was that these measures were all-important and would be proceeded with at once.
May I draw your attention to a further fact, Mr. Speaker. Not only did I point out that the measures for social reform and reform of the capitalistic system might be all-important, but I pointed out these were matters relating to the future and that important as they might be they should not be so placed as to sidetrack the immediate consideration of the problem of unemployment as we have it today, and the suffering to which as a consequence many people are being subjected. I did that because at every session of this parliament the discussion of the important question of unemployment has been left either to the very end of the session or until a moment immediately preceding an adjournment, such as the Easter recess. Never have we been able to get the government to permit discussion of supply of the Department of Labour or of a discussion of unemployment relief measures until a time approaching the very end of the session when hon. members had little or no opportunity for discussion. I do not think if we are able to avoid it we should permit that sort of thing to happen again. We should not allow the government to take up the time of this house from day to day in a discussion as to what supply the government is to get when at the same time all-important questions concerning the present difficulties of our people remain untouched. In the circumstances I believe we should ask that the all-important measures be proceeded with immediately.
May I draw the attention of the house to the fact that notwithstanding the offers of cooperation to expedite the introduction of reform measures the time of the house up to the present has been consumed by a consideration of measures other than those of the class I have mentioned. We have given first and second readings to an act to amend the Interpretation Act, an act to amend the Representation Act, an act to amend the criminal code and an act to amend the Pension Act. We have reached the second reading of Bill No. 2. an act to amend the Precious Metals Marking Act, and have reached the same stage on Bill No. 7, an act to amend and consolidate the acts relating to patents of invention. We have reached the committee of the whole with respect to one or two resolutions that appear on the order paper. None of these things are part of the all-important program of social and industrial reform.
[Mr. Mackenzie King.}

speechtext: They are part of public business, but may I tell the Minister of Railways that this house was called for the purpose of considering above all else these questions of social and industrial reform?

maintopic: SUPPLY-REFORM MEASURES AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF THE MINISTER OF JUSTICE FOR COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY
speechtext: So it will.

maintopic: SUPPLY-REFORM MEASURES AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF THE MINISTER OF JUSTICE FOR COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY
speechtext:
So it will, but, if it is within the power of some hon. members to have it so, it will do so at the earliest possible date, and not at the last moment.
Now may I make one point very clear, because I think it is just as well the public should understand what apparently the government has in mind, and what remarks such as those we have just heard from the other side of the house would indicate to be the case. The Prime Minister in his first broadcast over the radio on January 2, after intimating that he was going to outline to parliament the various measures of reform that were essential said, addressing the public:
I will then invite your considered opinion as to whether reform is in fact necessary.
Now this means after the session is all over. Do not forget that, Mr. Speaker. There is no undertaking that any of these measures are to be put into force before a general election. According to the Prime Minister's own statement to the public this house is to be kept going until, to appearances at all events, he can get this legislation on the statute books, and then there is to be a general election:
I will then invite your considered opinion as to whether reform is in fact necessary, and as to whether my program of reform is wise. If you say yes, then I will not rest until I have put it into operation.
It is quite easy to see what is in the Prime Minister's mind-a program of social reform to be put on the statutes, but none of it put into force. Then when we have a general election, the electorate is to be told: If you want this program of social reform you must support me. But even if they do support him the Prime Minister has not promised even then that he will put the program into force, because he says:
If you say yes, then I will not rest until I have put it into operation.

maintopic: SUPPLY-REFORM MEASURES AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF THE MINISTER OF JUSTICE FOR COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY
speechtext:
He will perish in the
attempt.

maintopic: SUPPLY-REFORM MEASURES AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF THE MINISTER OF JUSTICE FOR COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY
speechtext:
That is the
kind of thing he said all through the last election with respect to what he was going

Reform Measures-Mr. Mackenzie King
to do-that he would see these things were done, that he would not rest. We all agree he will not rest; he never will rest; but that does not mean that as a consequence any or all of these measures will ever be put into operation. I do not think the public should be humbugged with regard to any of this legislation, and so far as it is within the power of hon. gentlemen on this side to see that the situation is properly understood, we shall endeavour to see that the program of legislation is brought down, that it is stated in full, that it is carefully considered, and also that the conditions on which it is being proposed are understood by the public.
May 1 point out further, Mr. Speaker, that nothing could afford a stronger reason for not proceeding with consideration of supply until we have these measures before us than the Prime Minister's own declarations over the radio. I am going to read a few of these to hon. gentlemen, and I shall leave them and the country to consider whether we are not right in the circumstances in asking that these measures of reform should receive precedence over the less important business of the house, the kind of business my hon. friend the Minister of Railways has just referred to, such bills as those we have up to the present been considering, whether we should not instead give precedence to these allimportant measures of reform.
May I point out that these measures, if they are to be what we are told they are to be, are likely to be very, very far-reaching? This house will have to consider these measures very carefully. The Prime Minister tells us that one of them relating to unemployment insurance the government has been considering for over a year past. Well, the government may have been considering it that long, but all hon. members who are not of the cabinet have not had a chance to consider it at all, and we shall want a little time after the bill is brought down to consider its merits and to understand its implications.
It is altogether probable that these measures will involve careful consideration of vexatious questions of jurisdiction. How these difficulties may be most effectively met will have to be a subject of careful consideration. It is also probable that they will involve a very large expenditure of public money. Now where is this public money to come from? How it is to be raised will be an all-important question which the public will wish to have answered before it will be prepared to support or condemn any legislation. We have heard over and over again from the Prime
Minister himself the statement that if Canada's credit goes, everything is gone. We have also heard the statement that we cannot have social legislation given effect to to any appreciable extent on borrowed money, that the revenues of the country will have to be sufficient to meet its demands. Well up to the present ever since the present administration assumed office we have done little . but add to our public debt very, very considerably every year. We have increased taxation every year, and if these social measures are to be enacted and enforced the country will wish to know whether they are to be put in force on borrowed money or whether the money for them is to come out of increased taxation-at all events where the money is to come from which is to enable them to be effective.
These are matters that cannot be settled in a day or two, and we shall wish to have them very fully discussed here.
I want to make the position perfectly clear. We do not intend if we can avoid it, those of us who sit on this side of the house, to be put in the position of being dallied along from day to day, and week to week, with regard to these alleged measures of reform, only to find ourselves a month or two months hence without any real discussion of the measures, some of them not even then perhaps brought down, faced with a general election suddenly sprung on the country by the Prime Minister on the score that he has been meeting with nothing but opposition to the measures he has brought down. We do not intend to be put in that position. We intend to offer all we can in the way of helpful cooperation to measures that deserve the support of all parties in this house, but we must reserve to ourselves the right, which hon. members of every party should consider an obligation, to have every one of these measures before us in plenty of time to consider its provisions upon their merits and to give a straightforward and unbiased opinion with respect to each.
Having said this much, let me now read from what the Prime Minister said over the radio, because the Prime Minister's own words constitute one of the main reasons why I propose to move an amendment at the conclusion of my remarks, which I hope the house will deem it advisable to support.
Here is what the Prime Minister said in his second radio speech on January 4:
Now that the time has come to carry through a policy of reform, does any earnest-minded person say we should delay?
Well, we are all earnest-minded here, and we say there should be no delay. We agree
252	COMMONS
Reform, Measures-Mr. Mackenzie King
with the Prime Minister that these measures should be ready now, and we are prepared to consider them immediately. Next the Prime Minister said:
Now that we have achieved' some measure of control over economic conditions and can operate without fear of imminent disaster, we are going to do away as quickly as possible with emergency relief measures and put in a permanent system of sound and scientific insurance against unemployment.
When a Prime Minister tells the public even before parliament meets, that the government is going to do away as quickly as possible with emergency relief measures I say that the time for us to consider what is going to take their place is right now, not after we have been in supply a couple of weeks or a couple of months, or after a general election, but immediately. That is the most important problem; what is to take the place of relief measures, we want to know what the government's policies are with respect to unemployment relief and finding work for the unemployed. We want to know that as it relates to this year, the present time, and as it affects people throughout this country from the Atlantic to the Pacific. The Prime Minister says:
We are going to put in a permanent system of sound and scientific insurance against unemployment.
How long is it going to take that system; to get into operation? May I ask this question. How much help is a contributory system of unemployment insurance going to be to the man who has no employment at all and nothing to contribute? These are the people who have to be considered first of all, the people who have no work at all. This is insurance against unemployment in years to come; but what the country has needed during the last five years has been some method of providing work and relief, and we have not had any consistent policy on these two matters since the present government came into office.
Then take radio address, No. 3, delivered on January 7, here is an extract:
My friends, I have declared for reform. Now that the time for action has come, delay is hazardous. A machine which is out of adjustment must be repaired or it will cease to operate. We have decided that permanent prosperity waits upon reform measures.
Now, can we afford to delay reform measures when the Prime Minister tells us that permanent prosperity waits upon them? Can we afford to delay the consideration of these measures when the Prime Minister says that, now that the time for action has come, delay is hazardous? We are prepared

to take him at his word and to consider these measures as soon as the government brings them down. In the same speech the Prime Minister also said:
I say we must go quickly forward with our reform measures.

maintopic: SUPPLY-REFORM MEASURES AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF THE MINISTER OF JUSTICE FOR COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY
speechtext: Hear, hear.

maintopic: SUPPLY-REFORM MEASURES AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF THE MINISTER OF JUSTICE FOR COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY
speechtext:
An hon. member on the other side says "hear, hear." Well then, come on with them; we have not had any of the reform measures yet. This house was called together a week ago last Thursday and we are now in the third week of the session, but we have not had so far any of the reform .measures though the Prime Minister says that we should go quickly forward with them. I am only taking him at his word. What is another statement he made?
When some of you ask me, as you may: "why all this haste?" I say that, as a matter of fact, there is no haste at all, either in thought or action. There is urgency, but that is another matter. This is the right time for reform. We are now ready for it. We have been preparing for it.
So when the Minister of Justice asks me why I use the word "immediately", when the Minister of Railways asks, to all intents and purposes, why the haste, seeing that we have other public business on the order paper, I reply in the words of the Prime Minister:
There is urgency, but that is another matter. This is the right time for reform. We are now ready for it. We have been preparing for it.
Take radio address No. 4, delivered on January 9:
I have outlined our general policy of reform, and have indicated some of the measures in it which will be undertaken without delay.
That is all we are asking. This House has taken up all private members' resolutions, or at any rate, all have been called and most of them discussed, and we have concluded the debate on the address, so that we come now inevitably again to government measures, which of course have been called earlier than this. But the government is now again calling a government order and we ask hon. gentlemen opposite to call those measures which the Prime Minister says are all important and not to call supply at this stage, since that may mean only a method of postponing the discussion of more important questions. Further on, the same evening, the Prime Minister said:
We must go forward with our reform program, with speed and determination.
If this language means anything it means that we should not be losing time, allowing one week to pass, and another, and a third

Reform Measures-Mr. Guthrie
week to come without touching a single measure of reform. That is neither speed nor determination. On the same evening the Prime Minister said:
In my judgment, as I have said, we can expect little more progress without reform. On the contrary, there is a danger that we may go back and go back quickly, if we do not act decisively.
Surely in these circumstances no exception should be taken to a motion which proposes that all-important social reforms should be given precedence over other matters so that we may go forward and act decisively.
