He has the speed of
Balaam's ass.

maintopic: SUPPLY-REFORM MEASURES AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF THE MINISTER OF JUSTICE FOR COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY
speechtext:
Let me next
refer to radio address No. 5, delivered on January 11, 1935. The Prime Minister in that speech made the following statement:
You know that my whole program is by no means complete. The first stage has been well begun. The second stage we will immediately initiate.
May I ask the Minister of Justice to listen to this. He asked me a moment ago why I used the word "immediately," and I gave him many synonyms and equivalents in the Prime Minister's language. But the Prime Minister himself used that very word. It was the second stage that was to contain the program set forth in the speech from the throne. The first stage was comprised in those other measures that were	referred	to	as	having
already contributed towards recovery.
Now I come to	the last	of	the	broadcasts from Ottawa, which was on the night of January 15, two days before parliament assembled. It was	reported	in	the	morning papers the day before parliament met, and in this ' broadcast the Prime Minister speaks about what	will be	in	the	speech
from the throne, and the reason it will be there. And what does he say?
When the speech from the throne is read Thursday, you will find that we are taking steps to deal with these problems not next year but right now. We cannot accomplish everything at a single thrust but we can start, and we start now.
Well, that being the Prime Minister's wish in the matter, and those of us in the opposition desiring to cooperate with the government in these matters of social reform, I move, seconded by Mr. Mackenzie (Vancouver) :
That all the words in the motion after the word "that" be struck out and the following substituted therefor:
"This house is of the opinion that the immediate consideration of present conditions of unemployment and the introduction of measures
of social and industrial reform should not be delayed or postponed by a consideration of supply in advance of the consideration of government policies with respect to unemployment and the introduction of measures with respect to social and industrial reform."
In moving that amendment, may I repeat what I said at the outset, that at any time, once we have these measures before us and an opportunity given to consider them, if they are brought down promptly, we shall be prepared to have a group of hon. members on this side sit down with a group of hon. gentlemen opposite with respect to supply, to work out some means whereby the discussion of supply may be considerably limited, and the government in no way embarrassed in getting what is absolutely necessary.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: SUPPLY-REFORM MEASURES AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF THE MINISTER OF JUSTICE FOR COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY
speechtext:
I can only say that I think my
right hon. friend (Mr. Mackenzie King) exhibits too much concern in regard to the conduct of business in the House of Commons during the present session. I am inclined to think that he imagines, for some reason or other, that during the present session he is leading the house, but it was made abundantly clear to him by the Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett) a few days ago that the Prime Minister is still leading the House of Commons and proposes to direct the business of this chamber. What is the actual situation? The house undertook the transaction of business one week ago to-day, and to allay any fears on the part of the leader of the opposition I think I can state to him that perhaps the most important, or one of the most important, of the reform measures which have been announced in the speech from the throne will be under discussion in this chamber tomorrow. This is the first time in a long experience in this parliament that I have known an important government measure to be brought down within the first seven or eight days of the session.
Let me point out another matter to my right hon. friend. If any time has been wasted in this house during the past six days of its sitting it has not been wasted by members upon the government side.

maintopic: SUPPLY-REFORM MEASURES AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF THE MINISTER OF JUSTICE FOR COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY
speechtext:
What
about the flag debate?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: SUPPLY-REFORM MEASURES AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF THE MINISTER OF JUSTICE FOR COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY
speechtext:
It is all very well for my
right hon. friend to enumerate five or six bills as he did in his speech to-night, and to announce that all those bills have been given a second reading during the past week. The time of the house consumed in connection

Reform Measures-Mr. Guthrie
with all those bills was in the neighbourhood of half an hour, and my right hon. friend himself consumed more than five times that amount of time in a single speech in this chamber last week. If there has been any blocking, if there has been any delay, it is not attributable in any way to the government or to anything members of the government or members on this side of the house have done. There has been no delay; there has been no loss of time, but there has been every expedition on the part of the government to get the business of parliament under way.
I may have been misled during the course of the afternoon but I certainly was informed by one of my colleagues that it was prearranged that we should go into supply tonight for the purpose of opening two or three departments.

maintopic: SUPPLY-REFORM MEASURES AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF THE MINISTER OF JUSTICE FOR COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY
speechtext: Who made the arrangement?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: SUPPLY-REFORM MEASURES AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF THE MINISTER OF JUSTICE FOR COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY
speechtext: I am stating the information that was given to me.

maintopic: SUPPLY-REFORM MEASURES AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF THE MINISTER OF JUSTICE FOR COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY
speechtext:
Speaking for
the opposition I say that no arrangement of the kind was ever made or mentioned.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: SUPPLY-REFORM MEASURES AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF THE MINISTER OF JUSTICE FOR COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY
speechtext:
I may have been misled,
but I was certainly informed that by arrangement we would go into supply to-night for the purpose of opening two or three departments in order that later on in the week or later on in the session the house might at all times have business to occupy it.

maintopic: SUPPLY-REFORM MEASURES AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF THE MINISTER OF JUSTICE FOR COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY
speechtext: I do not think the hon. member ought to leave any such implication. I think he ought to ask his colleague where he got his information.

maintopic: SUPPLY-REFORM MEASURES AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF THE MINISTER OF JUSTICE FOR COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY
speechtext: There was no arrangement.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: SUPPLY-REFORM MEASURES AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF THE MINISTER OF JUSTICE FOR COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY
speechtext:
My colleague is not in
the house at present but I shall ask him. I accept my right hon. friend's denial. I perhaps have been misled but certainly that was my understanding of the situation.
Let me point this out also: My right hon. friend is well aware that this particular bill to which he referred, which is the unemployment insurance bill, is a difficult and complicated measure. He says that as soon as it is introduced the opposition will have to ask for time to consider it. That is reasonable. We were preparing so that in the meantime when the opposition were examining and considering the bill, this house would have something to occupy its time. It was for that particular reason the motion to go into supply 
was launched to-night, in order that we might be able to consider estimates during any interval which my right hon. friend might require to study the measure.

maintopic: SUPPLY-REFORM MEASURES AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF THE MINISTER OF JUSTICE FOR COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY
speechtext: Let us get the measure first.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: SUPPLY-REFORM MEASURES AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF THE MINISTER OF JUSTICE FOR COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY
speechtext: The resolution was placed promptly on the order paper, and unless something unforeseen happens, will be debated in the house to-morrow and the bill will be introduced to-morrow. I have rather gained the impression from the speech which was delivered in the house to-night that my right hon. friend is going through a period of preliminary training for one of the addresses which he is going to make over the radio later on. His speech sounded to me very much as a sort of preparation for something of the kind and did not have what one might call a genuine ring. He knows he cannot make out any case charging the government with delay at this early date in the session. The facts are entirely against him. When this bill is brought down others of a similar nature will follow it in due course and I suppose when they are introduced time will have to be allowed to the opposition for their consideration. In the meantime what business is there to occupy the house? Why not proceed in the usual way with the business of parliament? My right hon. friend may depend upon it that every measure forecast in the speech from the throne, every measure forecast in the radio addresses to which he has referred, will be promptly laid before parliament, and. I can assure my right hon. friend, will be enacted into law by this parliament at this session despite criticisms and despite objections. Why, when we looked in the paper this morning we found that my right hon. friend's chief lieutenant in Ontario, the premier of that province, had already condemned our whole program as unconstitutional and had raised many and various objections to it, I assume that he did so under instruction and I perhaps may assume also that such is going to be the course of my right hon. friend and his party in this house.

maintopic: SUPPLY-REFORM MEASURES AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF THE MINISTER OF JUSTICE FOR COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY
speechtext: I rise to a point of order. The Minister of Justice (Mr. Guthrie) has made more than an insinuation; he has made a direct charge. May I say to him that I have had no communication whatever with the premier of Ontario with respect to any legislation of this parliament this year or any year.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: SUPPLY-REFORM MEASURES AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF THE MINISTER OF JUSTICE FOR COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY
speechtext:
I am very glad to have that assurance, and I certainly will accept it

Reform. Measures-Mr. Guthrie
at one hundred per cent. But let me tell my right hon. friend that the premier of Ontario, who was one of his bosom friends and one of his bosom supporters in this house, who according to newspaper reports had been called into conference with him in this city before he became premier and since, certainly on Saturday last made very definite pronouncements against all the reform measures which the Prime Minister proposed to introduce. He even threatened the people of this country with a tour by himself and his lieutenants from the Atlantic to the Pacific in opposition to these reform measures.

maintopic: SUPPLY-REFORM MEASURES AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF THE MINISTER OF JUSTICE FOR COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY
speechtext: My hon. friend knows all these measures have been broadcast during this year. I have not even seen or written to the premier of Ontario this year.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: SUPPLY-REFORM MEASURES AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF THE MINISTER OF JUSTICE FOR COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY
speechtext: I think it would be better if my right hon. friend would get up and repudiate the position taken by the premier of Ontario, but what I fear is that that gentleman has sounded the keynote of opposition to all these reform measures, not only in Ontario where he spoke but in the House of Commons from the opposition benches. I am not going to be critical about the use of the word "immediate." I think my right hon. friend knows why I interjected that word when I did.

maintopic: SUPPLY-REFORM MEASURES AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF THE MINISTER OF JUSTICE FOR COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY
speechtext: Yes, because it is a substitution for "to-morrow."

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: SUPPLY-REFORM MEASURES AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF THE MINISTER OF JUSTICE FOR COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY
speechtext: I think he knows it had reference to a certain change which he made in Hansard last week.

maintopic: SUPPLY-REFORM MEASURES AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF THE MINISTER OF JUSTICE FOR COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY
speechtext: Yes, the Prime Minister spoke to me of a change in Hansard when he said I had used the word "immediate" and was putting words into his mouth. The word the Prime Minister used when he was introducing the resolution was that "to-morrow" he would introduce a certain resolution. When I read Hansard, that word "to-morrow" was changed to "immediate," because the word "tomorrow" was used a week ago and "immediate" was the word necessary to give the sense required at that time. It was a perfectly legitimate change.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: SUPPLY-REFORM MEASURES AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF THE MINISTER OF JUSTICE FOR COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY
speechtext: It was in reference to making that change in Hansard, putting words he had never used into the Prime Minister's mouth, that I objected to the word "immediate."

maintopic: SUPPLY-REFORM MEASURES AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF THE MINISTER OF JUSTICE FOR COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY
speechtext:
The minister is referring to something the Prime Minister spoke to me about in confidence, he said,
when I explained the change and he understood it quite well. I am glad my hon. friend has come out with what he said.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: SUPPLY-REFORM MEASURES AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF THE MINISTER OF JUSTICE FOR COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY
speechtext: The Prime Minister has not discussed with me anything he has discussed with my right hon. friend. The matter came to my notice in another way; but that was the reason for the interjection of the word "immediate." The Prime Minister has stated time and again in his broadcast speeches that he is going to lose no time, that he is going to act quickly. To-morrow he will introduce one of the main measures in the house. We have only had one week of actual business sessions; we started a week ago to-day. If that is not prompt enough for anyone I do not know what promptitude is in parliamentary action. No government I ever heard of has brought down measures as promptly as that. This measure will be followed from day to day or every few days by other measures in the reform program. No one in this chamber or out of it will have any cause to complain of delay in regard to these matters. The object and intention of the government is to press these measures with all haste. There will be expedition, not delay. We realize that these measures will probably require much consideration and discussion. But the bills will be offered to the house just as rapidly as it is possible to prepare and submit them. The unemployment insurance bill will be introduced to-morrow. I think probably as far as this side of the house is concerned we shall be prepared to go right on with it, but I am sure that will not suit the convenience of hon. members opposite. Well, what shall we go on with in the meantime unless you proceed with supply and let us consider supply from day to day when not otherwise occupied? The object in moving this motion to-night was merely to have some work on hand in case we are asked to delay consideration of these bills when they come down. But I repeat that up to the present moment there has not been a moment's delay. The work of the house has progressed according to the order paper as it progresses every session, perhaps more speedily than usual. If time has been wasted in the house it has not been by members on this side. If there has been obstruction it has not come from this side of the house.

maintopic: SUPPLY-REFORM MEASURES AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF THE MINISTER OF JUSTICE FOR COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY
speechtext: There has been no obstruction.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: SUPPLY-REFORM MEASURES AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF THE MINISTER OF JUSTICE FOR COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY
speechtext:
And if there are any
measures that have been passed or considered that are in any way objectionable I do not
256	COMMONS
Reform Measures-Mr. Woodsworth
know of them. We have acted regularly according to the rules and traditions of parliament, and we shall speed up all our reform measures and pass them with all the dispatch that this house will permit. Therefore I say that I think the criticism by the leader of the opposition to-night is entirely unfounded.

speakeroldname: Mr. J. S. WOODSWORTH (Winnipeg North Centre):
maintopic: SUPPLY-REFORM MEASURES AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF THE MINISTER OF JUSTICE FOR COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY
speechtext:
Some of us who do not
belong to either of the major parties in this house find ourselves in somewhat of a predicament when a motion of this kind is offered. I think we are just as anxious as anyone to have the business of the house speeded up. I think no one will accuse us of doing anything to prevent the earliest possible consideration of such questions as unemployment and social and industrial reform. I know that I personally want those measures brought in at the earliest possible moment. We have been trying to say that for the last four yeara. I think that the government have been very dilatory indeed in that they have left these measures until the last session of this parliament, but as far as this session is concerned I do not think anyone can say that the government have been slow in bringing down these measures. Due partly to the fact that a good many on this side have refused to take part in the debate on the address we are ready now to go on with them. Now we have a definite assurance from the Minister of Justice (Mr. Guthrie), representing the government, that this important measure of unemployment insurance will be brought down to-morrow, and that the other measures will be brought down in quick succession; that there will be no delay whatever. Under these circumstances I cannot very well vote in favour of the amendment. Personally I do not like opening up a number of departments, for the reason that in the past very frequently when a number of departments have been opened up we have found that our opportunity to raise questions on going into supply has been curtailed, and further, very frequently the government has passed rapidly from one department to another. That may have been convenient for the government, but it has not been convenient for all the members of the house. In practice most of us find it impossible to attend throughout every session when estimates are being put through. It seems to me there ought to be the fullest information given as to when the estimates of any particular department will be brought down, so that we shall not be absent when some estimate in which we are particularly interested is up for discussion. The number of departments opened at one time ought to

be very limited. But it does not seem to me an unreasonable proposal that the minister should open up a department or two to-night so that business could be carried on.
I know it is quite possible that if some of us vote against this amendment we may be accused of lacking interest in bringing in reforms; that kind of party trick has often been played. We may I think face that risk in view of the very definite assurances that have been given us by the Minister of Justice to-night.

speakeroldname: Hon. R. J. MANION (Minister of Railways and Canals):
maintopic: SUPPLY-REFORM MEASURES AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF THE MINISTER OF JUSTICE FOR COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I do not feel like sitting quietly here while the right hon. gentleman (Mr. Mackenzie King) endeavours to impress upon this house the great desire he has at this late time, after four and a half years of opposition, to put into effect reforms which he never proposed, which were proposed by the leader of the government (Mr. Bennett), but which the leader of the opposition now finds so important for this country that he thinks the ordinary business of our nation that every parliament deals with when it meets should be neglected, and we rush forward with every item of legislation which the government has to propose in order to give him a greater chance to criticize and oppose it.
Since this house first met we have had six business days. It is true there was the first Thursday, which was not a business day, and then on Friday there were the obituaries. But last week there were five days and to-day makes the sixth. Yet the right hon. leader of the opposition has the temerity to tell this house and the country that the Prime Minister delays bringing down his reform measures which he and every one except the right hon. gentleman knows to be necessary if this country is to survive and if the capitalistic system, in which I believe, and in which I think the right hon. leader of the opposition and indeed the majority of the people of this country believe, is to survive. The right hon. gentleman, not only to-day but during his speech on the address, has emphasized that his one object is to cooperate in these measures that the Prime Minister has proposed. He has said over and over again: Bring down these measures so that we can cooperate with the Prime Minister and the government in putting them through. But it is quite obvious to any observant person in this house and out of it that it is not his desire to cooperate, but that the desire of the right hon. gentleman is to embarrass. That is his whole object. And the right hon. gentleman knows it.

maintopic: SUPPLY-REFORM MEASURES AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF THE MINISTER OF JUSTICE FOR COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY
speechtext:
That is not fair.

Reform Measures-Mr. Mavion

maintopic: SUPPLY-REFORM MEASURES AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF THE MINISTER OF JUSTICE FOR COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY
speechtext: The trouble with the right hon. gentleman is that he has been scooped by the Prime Minister. For four and a half years the right hon. gentleman led the opposition and during that time neither he nor his party made one constructive proposal. They opposed everything the government proposed; they criticized at all times; they found fault with every piece of legislation that was brought in. They opposed the marketing bill.

maintopic: SUPPLY-REFORM MEASURES AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF THE MINISTER OF JUSTICE FOR COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY
speechtext: We did not.

maintopic: SUPPLY-REFORM MEASURES AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF THE MINISTER OF JUSTICE FOR COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY
speechtext:
They opposed the marketing bill when it was brought in. Half the party over there are on record as being opposed to the empire trade agreements, which opposition the right hon. gentleman is now trying to get out from underneath. They opposed practically everything the government brought into the house, but now, when the right hon. leader of the government has had the vision and courage to see that there must be corrections made to remedy the defects of the so called1 capitalistic system and to bring forward those corrections and propose them to the people of this country, the right hon. leader of the opposition, who had hoped to float into power on a tide of discontent and unrest, finds that he is scooped, and he has not been able to restrain his temper since he came into the house this session.
My right hon. friend now says that these reforms are all important, that we must put them through because the country needs them, and that the opposition wants to help get them through. These reforms, which he now finds so all-important, are the reforms which he never mentioned during the last four and a half years. I cannot say, of course, what he intends to do when the election comes around, but I do know that about a month ago the right hon. gentleman and his party had a conference here in this city. They met right in the city of Ottawa; they were here for two days; they had representatives from all over the country. The hon. member for Vancouver Centre (Mr. Mackenzie) was here; I think the hon. member for Quebec East (Mr. Lapointe) was here. There were representatives from the Atlantic to the Pacific, and what was the result?

maintopic: SUPPLY-REFORM MEASURES AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF THE MINISTER OF JUSTICE FOR COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY
speechtext: A mouse.

maintopic: SUPPLY-REFORM MEASURES AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF THE MINISTER OF JUSTICE FOR COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY
speechtext:
Yes, the mountain laboured and brought forth a mouse, or two mice in fact. The first mouse was a speech by the right hon. gentleman on world peace-of all subjects, as though there was anyone in God's green world except perhaps a few people in central Europe who wanted anything but 92582-17
world peace. At any rate the right hon. gentleman made a speech on world peace, and then they brought in a resolution condemning and abusing the government and demanding an immediate election, in mid-winter. That was the result of a two day conference here in the city of Ottawa, held about a month ago. Now, however, the right hon. gentleman says these are the all important measures; bring them forward and let us clean them up.
As it happened I have kept a few extracts which I happened to see in some of the newspapers during the last few weeks, since the right hon. Prime Minister submitted his program to the country. From those records let us see what some of the right hon. gentleman's lieutenants thought of these all important measures. Perhaps it would be a good thing to remind the right hon. gentleman and his friends of just what has been said. I have quotations here from speeches by a number of provincial members, but I need not read them. The first quotation I should like to give, perhaps because I like the hon. gentleman best, is by the hon. member for Quebec South (Mr. Power).

maintopic: SUPPLY-REFORM MEASURES AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF THE MINISTER OF JUSTICE FOR COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY
speechtext: Hear, hear.

maintopic: SUPPLY-REFORM MEASURES AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF THE MINISTER OF JUSTICE FOR COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY
speechtext:
Here is what he had to say:
Major Power of Quebec assails "Bennett's buncombe and humbug."
That is what he considered it to be. He thought the unemployment relief measures, the measures having to do with the limiting of hours of labour and minimum wages, and all the other reform measures proposed by the right hon. Prime Minister, were "Bennett's buncombe and humbug," yet the right hon. leader of the opposition stands up to-night and says let us get on with these important measures, so which are we to believe?
The next hon. member I should like to quote, and another whom I like very much also, is the hon. member for Ontario (Mr. Moore). That hon. gentleman is usually very careful in what he says; he is a very able supporter, perhaps the ablest on the other side, of the party which supports laissez-faire.

maintopic: SUPPLY-REFORM MEASURES AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF THE MINISTER OF JUSTICE FOR COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY
speechtext: He writes books too.

maintopic: SUPPLY-REFORM MEASURES AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF THE MINISTER OF JUSTICE FOR COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY
speechtext:
Yes, and very interesting
books; I read the last two and enjoyed them very much. He says Mr. Bennett's speeches are a very ordinary election appeal. Again these are the measures which the right hon. leader of the opposition says are so allimportant. The hon. member for Ontario calls this program a very ordinary election

258	COMMONS
Reform Measures-Mr. Manion
appeal, while his right hon. leader says for God's sake let us get them brought down, let us get at them and put them through, because the country needs them.
Then my genial friend from Vancouver Centre stopped off at every place across the continent to make a speech. He was not satisfied to condemn the Prime Minister and all his words and works out in Vancouver; he got off even in my own city to make a speech. Every time he passes through he honours me by stopping off in Fort William; he likes me so much that he wants to help elect me. I am sure he has been helping me; I know he thinks I am going to be elected, because he told me so. I hope I may be forgiven for quoting him, but he told me so, and I do not know any better proof that I am reasonably sure of election.

maintopic: SUPPLY-REFORM MEASURES AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF THE MINISTER OF JUSTICE FOR COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY
speechtext:
Perhaps the hon. member
introduced him to Miss Lizzie Fair.

maintopic: SUPPLY-REFORM MEASURES AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF THE MINISTER OF JUSTICE FOR COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY
speechtext:
No, he was not the
gentleman. The hon. member got off at Fort William and called Mr. Bennett's proposal "a new deal or a new steal." That was what he termed it; that was his opinion. Even the youngest member of the house, the hon. member for North York (Mr. Mulock) jumped into the limelight and put himself on record as condemning not only the Prime Minister but also his own leader, because his own leader says to-night, as he said on Friday and last Monday and every time he was on his feet, almost with tears in his eyes and with an appeal to this house, "For heaven's sake let us get on with these measures. The country needs them. We are anxious to shove aside all the rest of the business of the house in order to get on with them." But the hon. member for North York says:
"Confederation threatened by Bennett," states Mulock. Condemns Prime Minister for his audacity and impudence.
The hon. member condemns the Prime Minister, forsooth. I am afraid the people of this country will have to decide which is showing the audacity and impudence. According to the report I have, during this speech at Aurora the hon. member said:
Premier Bennett's policies will "break up confederation because his ambition is to set up a dictatorship," charged Colonel W. P. Mulock, M.P. for North York riding at a meeting of prominent Liberals at his farm here last night. "He thought he was the second Barnum-"
He is speaking of Mr. Bennett.
"-but he is going to be mistaken."

maintopic: SUPPLY-REFORM MEASURES AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF THE MINISTER OF JUSTICE FOR COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY
speechtext: In regard to the statement made by the minister-

maintopic: SUPPLY-REFORM MEASURES AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF THE MINISTER OF JUSTICE FOR COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY
speechtext:
Is the hon. member rising
to a point of order?

maintopic: SUPPLY-REFORM MEASURES AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF THE MINISTER OF JUSTICE FOR COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY
speechtext:
Yes. I should like to
correct the minister. I have no doubt that he is reading the quotation correctly, but I did not make that statement.

maintopic: SUPPLY-REFORM MEASURES AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF THE MINISTER OF JUSTICE FOR COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY
speechtext:
Then my hon. friend will
have to correct the Toronto Daily Star, from which I am quoting.

maintopic: SUPPLY-REFORM MEASURES AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF THE MINISTER OF JUSTICE FOR COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY
speechtext:
The minister
should accept the word of the hon. member.

maintopic: SUPPLY-REFORM MEASURES AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF THE MINISTER OF JUSTICE FOR COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY
speechtext:
Of course I accept my
hon. friend's statement, but I have quoted the Toronto Star, and that same newspaper quotes him a little further. He can correct this also if he wishes to do so. He said:
"Let us go out and save these liberties for which our forefathers gave their lives. Fight to make this country what Laurier and Mackenzie King made it."
The hon. member for Laurier-Outremont (Mr. Mercier) also made a speech, in which he said:
It certainly looks as though Mr. Bennett was preparing for the role of dictator.
Yet his leader says that these measures are so important that he wants to put them through without delay, so he cannot believe in this dictator business.
I could go on indefinitely, but I will quote only one other hon. member. These quotations are rather good; they may help my hon. friends in their campaign when the time comes. I have one quotation from Mr. Roebuck of the Ontario government, but I do not wish to read it; his was worst of all. Then even the senators got into it, because we find Senator Graham, my dear old friend George Graham, making statements. The following is an article which appeared in the press:
Asked what significance he attached to Mr. Bennett's failure to extend the attack to include the C.C.F., Mr. Graham believed Mr. Bennett hoped to attract the support of that body to himself, as he appeared to be adopting some of their platforms ... his program as far as one can understand, is in head-on collision with his former policies which, at the present time, are still adhered to by the Conservative party.
So even he found fault. I shall now quote some observations by the hon. member for Northumberland (Mr. Fraser) and then I shall stop quoting. I could go down the list of those who spoke, but I shall not take the time. The hon. member for Northumberland said:

Reform. Measures-Mr. Manion
Mr. Bennett's utterances are more fantastic than anything that ever came out of the Arabian Nights.
I should like hon. members on this side of the house to remember what the opinion of the Liberal party as constituted in this house is concerning proposals for reform. That is worth while remembering, and yet in spite of his lieutenants the right hon. gentleman says, "We must deal at once with these matters and put them on the statute books"- on the statute books, not in his book, "We must get them forward and have them in a position to carry them out."
I accept the right hon. gentleman's attitude, namely that these are very fine measures. I can draw only that conclusion, if I believe in his sincerity at all.

maintopic: SUPPLY-REFORM MEASURES AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF THE MINISTER OF JUSTICE FOR COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY
speechtext: I do not think my hon. friend has quite understood what I have said. He keeps saying that I have said these measures are excellent. I have been quoting the Prime Minister's statement that they are so necessary. What I have wanted is that we may see the measures which are so important, and if they deserve support they will get it. I cannot speak of the measures until I see them.

maintopic: SUPPLY-REFORM MEASURES AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF THE MINISTER OF JUSTICE FOR COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY
speechtext: The right hon. gentleman has been taking the stand that we should bring them down hurriedly.

maintopic: SUPPLY-REFORM MEASURES AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF THE MINISTER OF JUSTICE FOR COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY
speechtext: So we can see them.

maintopic: SUPPLY-REFORM MEASURES AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF THE MINISTER OF JUSTICE FOR COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY
speechtext:
Now he states the reason he has made statements is because he has been quoting the Prime Minister. He is not always so reasonable in taking the Prime Minister's word for things of that kind. He must have some use for them. If the right hon. gentleman does not think these measures are going to be of any use to the Dominion of Canada why is he in such a rush? Why is he trying to embarrass the government even to the extent of blocking supply, and offering an amendment to the motion to go into committee of supply so that the work of that committee may be delayed? Why has he objected to every little bill that has been introduced? Three or four of them were reported one afternoon, and they were passed in much less time than he took while speaking on the address in reply. Yet he keeps pushing things along. Now he wishes to withdraw from his position and apparently stands with the chap who said, "I am their leader; I must follow them." He has heard some of his followers and therefore he is going to follow them instead of precede them.
I say that the Prime Minister has shown vision and courage in bringing forward these 92582-174
reform measures, a vision and courage which' everybody, with the exception apparently of the leader of the opposition and some of his-colleagues, has recognized. At one time I did accept the right hon. gentleman's sincerity in his attempt to have the measures brought forward, but now it would seem he is trying even to back up from that. Therefore I do not know now whether I can accept his sincerity in the attitude he has taken in the house. I must state that, so far as I can see, his endeavours to hasten the measures of reform are not for the purpose of hastening reform but for the purpose of embarrassing the government. He is doing it for the purpose of killing time. The right hon. gentleman and his followers for the past four years have done nothing in this house but offer criticism during the most terrible crisis the world has ever gone through. In all those four years he has offered nothing by way of constructive suggestion. It is true that he has said on one occasion he suggested an interprovincial conference. Let me tell him we had three or four interprovincial conferences, and in most of them the provincial representatives went away agreeing unanimously with the policy of this government. So far as I can remember, and I speak in all sincerity, I know of no constructive suggestion the right hon. gentleman has offered in those four .years. In that time he and his party in this chamber have been just as useful to the country-and no more useful-than the drought in Saskatchewan.
I do not wish to take further time of the house, but I should like to say that the Prime Minister has not only recognized the need for reform, but in the four years in which he and his government have held office they have brought this country through the crisis in better condition than any country in the world. To that statement I make no exception. Not only Canada, but the rest of the world is going forward on the road to progress and prosperity, and the successful issue so far as Canada is concerned is due to the efforts of the Prime Minister. Now he is going to crown his work of four and a half years by these reform measures. I submit again to the right hon. leader of the opposition if he is the sincere friend of the country he says he is-and I wish to accept his statement, because I do not question any man's loyalty- if he is so sincere he will give the Prime Minister proper time; he will not endeavour to embarrass the government instead of attempting to assist it.

maintopic: SUPPLY-REFORM MEASURES AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF THE MINISTER OF JUSTICE FOR COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is always a great
pleasure to listen to an address by the Min-
260	COMMONS
Reform Measures-Mr. Stewart (Edmonton)
ister of Railways and Canals (Mr. Manion). Hon. members enjoy listening to him. He has the real Irish spirit, and on this occasion the hon. member has excelled himself. If ever there was a party which has swallowed itself, body, bones and breeches, certainly the Conservative party has done it on this occasion. They have not left a thing. They have even tried to steal the policies of my good friends sitting in the comer of the chamber.

maintopic: SUPPLY-REFORM MEASURES AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF THE MINISTER OF JUSTICE FOR COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY
speechtext:
We couldn't steal yours
because you didn't have any.

maintopic: SUPPLY-REFORM MEASURES AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF THE MINISTER OF JUSTICE FOR COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY
speechtext:
I say to the hon. member that that is exactly what he is trying to do. The Conservative party is trying to do that, and it is caught in the act. For four long years we have been trying to defend the people of Canada against the present administration. When the hon. member excites himself into one of his tirades I am reminded of the story of the Irishman who got drunk in New York. Being an Irishman the minister will appreciate this story; as it is against my own church and in favour of his I do not think he should object. Having spent the night in debauchery the Irishman decided the proper thing to do would be to go to church, and with that in mind he went to the little church around the corner. As there was a verger in the church the Irishman said to him. " When is mass about to begin ?" " Why," the verger replied ; " my dear friend, you are in the wrong place; this is not your church; it is an Anglican church." The Irishman looked around the walls and in one comer he saw a picture of our Saviour, and asked, " Is that not a picture of our Saviour up there in that niche?" The reply was in the affirmative. " Is that not a picture of the Mother in that niche?" The reply was again in the affirmative. "Is that not St. Peter over there?" "Yes it is." "Well then," said the Irishman, " since when did them folks become Protestants?" The change of heart my hon. friend has undergone in these four years is I believe described by that story, and in telling it I have had no desire to be profane. We have not heard the new policies yet, and that is why we have shown some anxiety. A few days ago the Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett) told us that the most important piece of legislation, which had on a former occasion been mentioned by the party in the comer of the chamber, was prepared as early as last March. Why was it not brought down? Why could it not have been brought down? As usual, did the right hon. gentleman want to do his stall-
[Mr. C. A. Stewart.!
ing trick? They want to delay. They need delay; the Lord knows they are going to need a lot of delay before they pass this legislation, because so far as I can discover it merely amounts to some amendments to Liberal policies of 1921.

maintopic: SUPPLY-REFORM MEASURES AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF THE MINISTER OF JUSTICE FOR COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY
speechtext: Oh, oh.

maintopic: SUPPLY-REFORM MEASURES AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF THE MINISTER OF JUSTICE FOR COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY
speechtext:
Well, I
shall be glad to see it when it comes down. I will go as far as to state that I will support anything which is in conformity with Liberal policies. Neither my hon. friend nor his leader has any right to go around this country and say that this party or my leader opposed the marketing act.

maintopic: SUPPLY-REFORM MEASURES AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF THE MINISTER OF JUSTICE FOR COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY
speechtext: The only member opposite who supported it was the hon. member for Melville (Mr. Motherwell).

maintopic: SUPPLY-REFORM MEASURES AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF THE MINISTER OF JUSTICE FOR COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY
speechtext: It does not make any difference what my hon. friend from Melville said. Time and again during the discussion of the marketing act it was made perfectly clear that we on this side of the house stood for cooperative marketing, but did we stand for the iniquitous provisions set out in that act? No, we did not, and we do not stand for them to-day. Did we stand for a board being set up in British Columbia with power to say, "You shall not ship Alberta butter into British Columbia?" No, we did not, and we do not stand for it to-day. We might just as well face this thing squarely. We are not going to be put in the position of having it said that we opposed the principle of the marketing act. We are not going to have that said either by the leader of the party opposite or by any hon. gentleman opposite. But we did oppose the provisions of that act.

maintopic: SUPPLY-REFORM MEASURES AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF THE MINISTER OF JUSTICE FOR COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY
speechtext: You opposed everything.

maintopic: SUPPLY-REFORM MEASURES AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF THE MINISTER OF JUSTICE FOR COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY
speechtext:
And we are prepared to oppose them again, because we opposed them in the interests of the people of this country.
Let me say to my hon. friends on the other side of the house that never in the history of Canada has there been a period of four years in which more damage was done than in the four years they have been in power. More men have lost their homes, not only in the urban centres but in the rural parts of Canada, and they are losing their homes to-day.

maintopic: SUPPLY-REFORM MEASURES AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF THE MINISTER OF JUSTICE FOR COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY
speechtext: And a million people on relief.

maintopic: SUPPLY-REFORM MEASURES AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF THE MINISTER OF JUSTICE FOR COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY
speechtext:
And they are losing their homes on account of the policies of this government.

Reform Measures-Mr. Stewart (Edmonton)

maintopic: SUPPLY-REFORM MEASURES AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF THE MINISTER OF JUSTICE FOR COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY
speechtext: Oh, oh.

maintopic: SUPPLY-REFORM MEASURES AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF THE MINISTER OF JUSTICE FOR COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY
speechtext:
Go out on
the prairies and see the procession taking place off the farms daily. In my own city of Edmonton hundreds of people have lost their homes through taxation and their inability to pay as they were unable to secure work. I am told on fairly good authority that over fifty per cent of the land of that city belongs to the municipality to-day. And then hon. gentlemen opposite get up and say that they are the authors of everything that saved the situation in Canada, and that Canada came out of the depression better than any other country. If that is true, and I question it, the people of Canada came out better because of their innate ability to withstand the legislation that this government offered.
Hon. gentlemen opposite get up and criticize my leader and accuse him of a policy of laissez-faire. The leader of the government the other day said that my leader did not know which side of the fence he was on. Lord knows I would like to know which side of the fence the Prime Minister is on. Nobody has jumped the fence quicker than he has done. I ask hon. gentlemen opposite to read his Christmas address to the people of Canada, and then to read his New Year's speech, and then his radio broadcasts. Just compare them, and then let us see if any hon. gentleman opposite will stand in his place and accuse anyone on this side of inconsistency. I cannot think of words sufficiently strong, Mr. Speaker, to do justice to the occasion.
My hon. friend the Minister of Railways gets up to-night and proceeds in his usual form to lecture the opposition for their tactics. Does he remember when he sat over here, and his good friend the ex-Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Stevens)?

maintopic: SUPPLY-REFORM MEASURES AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF THE MINISTER OF JUSTICE FOR COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY
speechtext: I have forgotten that.

maintopic: SUPPLY-REFORM MEASURES AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF THE MINISTER OF JUSTICE FOR COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY
speechtext: I sat on the government side of the house when my hon. friend the present Minister of Railways sat over here. Does he remember 1930?

maintopic: SUPPLY-REFORM MEASURES AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF THE MINISTER OF JUSTICE FOR COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY
speechtext: Sure I do.

maintopic: SUPPLY-REFORM MEASURES AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF THE MINISTER OF JUSTICE FOR COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY
speechtext:
Yes, I know he remembers, and then his right-about-face. He was following then the tactics of an opposition that are doing nothing more or less, and no one did that half as strongly as he and his leader did when they were sitting over here. Our business as an opposition is to scrutinize every piece of legislation that is brought down.
We have had broadcast announcements by the Prime Minister, not once but five times, about the legislation that is all ready, that is
going to reform the whole country, and God knows it needs it. In 1930 we had 117,000 unemployed, according to the statement issued by hon. gentlemen opposite, who were then in opposition, and to-day we have well over one million. '

maintopic: SUPPLY-REFORM MEASURES AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF THE MINISTER OF JUSTICE FOR COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY
speechtext: Nothing of the sort.

maintopic: SUPPLY-REFORM MEASURES AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF THE MINISTER OF JUSTICE FOR COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY
speechtext: Oh, no.

maintopic: SUPPLY-REFORM MEASURES AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF THE MINISTER OF JUSTICE FOR COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY
speechtext: To-day wes have one million on relief.

maintopic: SUPPLY-REFORM MEASURES AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF THE MINISTER OF JUSTICE FOR COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY
speechtext: That is different.

maintopic: SUPPLY-REFORM MEASURES AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF THE MINISTER OF JUSTICE FOR COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY
speechtext: Hon. gentlemen opposite talk about there being only 400,000 unemployed to-day. I venture to say to hon. gentlemen opposite, and I am sure I am supported by some of their own friends, that there are twice four hundred thousand unemployed.

maintopic: SUPPLY-REFORM MEASURES AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF THE MINISTER OF JUSTICE FOR COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY
speechtext: That is exaggerating.

maintopic: SUPPLY-REFORM MEASURES AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF THE MINISTER OF JUSTICE FOR COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY
speechtext:
They have just discovered that the young men coming out of the universities have to have a job. These young men have been out of jobs for four years, as hon. gentlemen know.
Then look at the speeches which the Prime Minister himself has made in previous sessions in favour of sound money and in defence of tariffs. We were told in those days to tighten our belts. That is all the satisfaction the people of this country got out of the situation up until a short while ago, and not until my good friend the ex-Minister of Trade and Commerce started his crusade was there any change of heart among hon. gentlemen opposite. He was the first one to see the light-and all credit to him for having seen it-and what happened to him? He is no longer in the government giving advice; but suddenly the government discovered that his program was going to be very acceptable to the people of this country and they thought it about time to make a right-about-face.
Now bring on your legislation. Let us have a look at it. You do not need to pass estimates. You do not require money until the thirty-first of March. But no. You have to admit now, after all this ballyhoo about reform measures-I know no better word, Mr. Speaker-that you do not yet know what you are going to do about this reform legislation. That is the plain, honest fact of the case. You do not know what you are going to introduce, except for the one measure that was prepared in March a year ago; and I am not stretching my imagination very much when I say that. We as an opposition are
262	COMMONS
Reform Measures-Mr. McPhee
entitled to know what you propose to introduce. We are entitled to know what you are going to do about it.
We realize the serious situation in this country to-day. I suppose I shall be accused of maligning Canada when I say that I for one believe that Canada is on the verge of bankruptcy. And what have hon. gentlemen opposite done? They have added to the public debt in every direction in the last four years. I say that advisedly, and if they do not change their tactics and stop adding to the public debt of this country we will be bankrupt. I am not saying anything more, Mr. Speaker, than was said by hon. gentlemen opposite in 1930 when they were sitting over here. I have taken the trouble to examine the situation, and I am going to say something more when the opportunity offers, with respect to the attitude of hon. gentlemen opposite in 1930.
Here they are trembling on the brink of an election, fearful of the electorate.

maintopic: SUPPLY-REFORM MEASURES AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF THE MINISTER OF JUSTICE FOR COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY
speechtext: Not trembling.

maintopic: SUPPLY-REFORM MEASURES AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF THE MINISTER OF JUSTICE FOR COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY
speechtext:
And you have a right to be afraid of the people. We were promised an early election but the latest reports are that the water does not look so good since the session started. Let me say to hon. gentlemen opposite: You are the government, and it is your responsibility to bring down the legislation. It is our responsibility to examine it, to criticize it where necessary and to agree to it when we believe it will help out the situation that is so serious in this country at the present time. I support my leader in everything he said to-night and I shall support him later on in connection with this matter.
I say to hon. gentlemen opposite: Bring *on your legislation and let us examine it. The only defence we have, the only weapon we can use, is to refuse you supply until we know what your program is, and1 that we propose to do.
Mr. GEORGE W. McPHEE (Yorkton): Mr. Speaker, with the hon. member for West Edmonton (Mr. Stewart) I agree. I happen to have sat on the other side of the house for nine years, and I well recall my red-blooded Irish Canadian friend on the other side of the house obstructing, when he was sitting over here, every bit of legislation that was 'brought down by tire government headed by the present right hon. leader of the opposition (Mr. Mackenzie King).
My hon. friend the Minister of Justice (Mr. Guthrie) to-night boasts that the legislation foreshadowed in the Prime Minister's (Mr. C. A. Stewart.]
fireside chats will be brought down immediately. He said the same thing in 1930, because I recall that in that year the Minister of Justice (Mr. Guthrie) made the statement in Winnipeg that in three days his leader would end unemployment if he were returned to power.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: SUPPLY-REFORM MEASURES AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF THE MINISTER OF JUSTICE FOR COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY
speechtext:
No; you never heard
that, and it never was said.

maintopic: SUPPLY-REFORM MEASURES AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF THE MINISTER OF JUSTICE FOR COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY
speechtext:
His right hon. leader was
a little more definite than that. He said, speaking at the same place in June, 1930: " I propose, if elected to power, to call a session of parliament"-one of the two promises he kept-" immediately after July 28, and to introduce national undertakings which will give work to our workmen. I propose to have immediately enacted such measures as will do away with the bogy of unemployment." That was in 1930. I was in Sherbrooke a year ago addressing a meeting there, and I was told by the labouring people of that city that the present leader of the government went there in 1930, a few days before the election, and made an address. In that beautiful city of 25,000 people he spoke as dramatically as he did when he delivered his fireside chats a week ago. They described to me the manner in which he walked out to the edge of the platform at three o'clock in the afternoon and said: "I know what is wrong with the good city of Sherbrooke. These factories, fifty of them built by the industry of its people, are not going full time. Men are being laid off. Put me in office and there will be work and work aplenty for every able-bodied man in Sherbrooke." What was the situation there when I addressed that meeting? There were 2,500 men in that city attending the soup kitchen.
The Minister of Railways boasts about the contrast between Liberal and Conservative governments in their attitude toward labour. Let me give him this illustration. In 1928 when the Liberal government reduced the duty on automobiles from 35 to 20 per cent, a reduction which was fought tooth and nail by the Minister of Railways and everyone on that side, 4,000 workmen from Oshawa came to this city. Those hon. members who were here at the time will remember what happened. They filled two blocks in front of these parliament buildings, and they carried banners. These banners indicated that they were returned men: "We fought for Canada and we want to make Canada our home." They thought that after this reduction went into effect they would lose their employment and would have to go elsewhere

Health Policy-Mr. Spencer
for work. What did my right hon. leader do? I want this house and the country to contrast the record of these two men, the present leader of the government and the present leader of the opposition. My leader on that occasion, in conjunction with the late Mr. Robb, then Minister of Finance, hired the largest theatre in the city, the Capitol theatre to which they requested that labour group to retire in orderly fashion. The men did so and they were addressed both by Mr. Robb and by the then leader of the government, the present leader of the opposition. I can hear Mr. Robb telling them, "Go back home, men. They will not close your factories. As a result of the reduction the factories will be working overtime and you will have more work." The men went back and the factories tvent on That is liberalism.

maintopic: SUPPLY-REFORM MEASURES AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF THE MINISTER OF JUSTICE FOR COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY
speechtext: It was never put into effect.

maintopic: SUPPLY-REFORM MEASURES AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF THE MINISTER OF JUSTICE FOR COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY
speechtext:
Contrast that with what has taken place in the last four years. What happened when farmers from the good old province of Ontario came here and assembled in the exhibition building? Neither the leader of the government nor any member of his government, nor anyone on his behalf, went to address those men. That is the way they treat the labouring people of this country-and after all farmers are labouring people. It reminds me of the late Sir Sam Hughes, a Conservative, and his attitude to a delegation of a thousand farmers from western Canada. He had the effrontery to describe these men as "this gang of leaders"- men whose wives were at home wearing long boots cleaning out stables and doing other laborious work while the men were down here pleading for lower tariffs on their necessities. Take the labour delegation that came to the House of Commons three years ago. The Prime Minister had promised "Come unto me all ye that labour and I will give you work" and they came to this city and assembled on Wellington street, a thousand strong. What happened? They were not even allowed to pass the gates. Far from being invited to go to a theatre where they could be seated comfortably they were not allowed to enter these grounds. Instead they were met by armed men. That is the contrast between liberalism and conservativ-ism so far as their respective relations with labour are concerned.
And now we have this spectacle of the Prime Minister of this country having promised eveiything under heaven four years ago, having all his life "insistently fought
for the capitalistic system, having profited as no other professional man in this country has profited as a result of that system-we find him now, not as Saul on the road to Damascus but as Richard Bedford on the road to his defeat, denouncing the very thing from which he has profited the most of any person in the country.

maintopic: SUPPLY-REFORM MEASURES AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF THE MINISTER OF JUSTICE FOR COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY
speechtext: Eleven o'clock.
What is the business to-morrow?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I assume that this dilatory motion will proceed until it is disposed of.

May I point
out that the government can arrange the order itself. If the government cares to introduce its legislation immediately it may have its effect on this motion.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: This dilatory motion may have to be disposed of; otherwise we will go on with government orders, taking up the resolution in the name of the Prime Minister in regard to unemployment insurance, and there is another resolution to follow.

At eleven o'clock the house adjourned without question put, pursuant to standing order.
Tuesday, January 29, 1935
